sessions.title: Vibe Coding and AI-Assisted Development
sessions.description: Build an intuitive understanding of 'vibe coding' as coined by Andrej Karpathy. Discover how expressing intent in natural language differs from manually writing syntax.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by introducing the revolutionary concept of 'Vibe Coding,' a term popularized by AI researcher Andrej Karpathy. Explain that traditional software development has always required a high cognitive tax: translating a creative human idea into rigid, machine-readable syntax like semicolons, curly braces, and memory management. Contrast this with 'Vibe Coding,' where the primary medium of creation is natural language. Emphasize that this is not about being lazy; it is a profound paradigm shift where the creator moves from being a manual typewriter to a high-level creative director. This introduction immediately lowers the barrier to entry for non-technical learners, framing their lack of coding experience not as a disadvantage, but as an opportunity to master system design without syntax baggage.

To make this concrete, draw a comparative grid diagram on the physical or virtual whiteboard. On the left column, label it 'Traditional Software Engineering' and map out its workflow: Ideation, Syntax Parsing, Manual Debugging, and Compiling. On the right column, label it 'Vibe Coding' and map out its workflow: Strategic Intent, Natural Language Prompting, AI Generation, and System Evaluation. Walk through the grid step-by-step to show how the bottle-neck of development has shifted. In traditional coding, hours are spent finding a missing comma; in vibe coding, hours are spent refining the clarity of your instructions. Use the metaphor of building a house: the traditional programmer is laying every brick by hand, whereas the vibe coder is the architect directing an automated construction crew.

Next, unpack the spectrum of automation by defining 'Full Vibe Coding' versus 'Human-Led Vibe Coding.' Explain that full vibe coding is an idealized state where an AI agent attempts to build an entire application with zero human oversight. Point out the danger of this extreme: without a human feedback loop, AI agents often fall into recursive hallucination loops, writing overly complex code to patch minor bugs. Contrast this with 'Human-Led Vibe Coding,' which is the focus of this course. In this model, the human acts as the pilot and critical evaluator, steering the AI, establishing design boundaries, and constantly checking if the application's performance matches the intended 'vibe.' This distinction prevents the common beginner pitfall of expecting the AI to magically read their mind.

Conclude the session with an interactive scenario-based reflection. Ask the audience to imagine they want to build a simple daily habit tracker. Guide them to visualize how a traditional developer would start by writing database schemas and setting up local servers. Then, show how a vibe coder would start by simply writing: 'Create a clean, minimalist web page where I can click a button to log my water intake.' This stark contrast reinforces the core takeaway of the lecture: vibe coding allows anyone to prototype at the speed of thought, provided they learn how to guide and evaluate the AI assistant effectively.

tasks: Contrast the mental workflow of a traditional programmer with that of a natural-language vibe coder using a comparative grid diagram.
Identify the core characteristics of full vibe coding vs human-led vibe coding.

sessions.title: What the AI Assistant Can Do
sessions.description: Examine the capabilities of modern AI coding assistants—from file creation and autocompletion to agentic generation of multi-file applications.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by establishing a clear mental spectrum of AI assistance on the whiteboard. Draw a horizontal axis representing the level of AI autonomy, ranging from basic 'Autocomplete' on the left, moving to 'Single-File Generation' in the middle, and reaching 'Agentic Multi-File Development' on the far right. Explain that understanding what the AI can do is not about memorizing commands, but about knowing where on this spectrum your current task falls. Address a common beginner misconception: that AI is either a magic mind-reader that builds entire companies in one click, or just a glorified search engine. By framing it as a scalable spectrum, you help students see that they can dial the AI's autonomy up or down depending on the complexity of the task.

Next, dive deep into the AI's natural sweet spots—the areas where it excels. On the whiteboard, list these under the heading 'The AI's Superpowers.' Explain that LLMs are exceptionally good at generating UI boilerplates, standard CSS styling, basic database schemas, and repetitive boilerplate code because these patterns exist in millions of open-source examples. Walk through the logic of why this is the case: the AI functions by predicting the most probable next token based on pattern recognition. Therefore, highly standardized tasks are trivial for it. Use the example of a landing page signup form—something the AI can generate flawlessly in seconds, saving the human hours of tedious layout work.

Shift the focus to the AI's blind spots, labeling this section on the whiteboard as 'The Steering Zone.' Explain that as tasks become highly customized, mathematically complex, or architecturally distributed across multiple files, the AI's probability-based generation begins to falter. Discuss the concept of 'context drift'—how an AI can lose track of the overall application architecture when forced to make too many assumptions at once. Illustrate this with a simple metaphor: if you ask an architect to build a house room-by-room without a master blueprint, the kitchen doors might eventually block the hallway. This explains why the human must step in to manage state coordination and overall project boundaries.

Conclude the session with an interactive classification exercise. Present the students with a list of six real-world development tasks: creating a basic button layout, implementing a complex custom payment routing logic, writing a standard JSON data parser, debugging an API error with no logs, scaffold-building a profile page, and optimizing a complex database query. Guide the students to categorize these into 'AI-Heavy Execution' or 'Human-Steered Strategy' columns on the whiteboard. This exercise is designed to test whether students can distinguish between tasks they can fully delegate to the vibe-coding workflow and tasks where they must remain actively engaged as the primary analytical director.

tasks: List three tasks an AI coder excels at (e.g., UI boilerplate) and three areas where it requires careful steering (e.g., highly custom complex state logic).

sessions.title: The Human's Role and Responsibility
sessions.description: Understand that the human is not a passive spectator. Explore the critical responsibility of being an auditor, controller, and decision-maker, setting up the mindset that AI output is always unverified until proven otherwise.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by dismantling the most common misconception of the AI era: the belief that natural-language coding turns the human into a passive passenger. In a concept-first public lecture style, the teacher must paint a vivid analogy of the human as a creative director or an editor-in-chief. Just as an editor-in-chief does not write every paragraph but is entirely responsible for the factual accuracy and overall quality of the newspaper, the vibe coder must realize that they own the final output. This mental shift is critical because modern AI models are optimized for plausibility rather than truth. They write beautiful, grammatically correct code that looks highly professional, which easily lulls beginners into a false sense of security. The primary goal of this introduction is to install a healthy skepticism, moving the learner from blind trust to active leadership.

To build intuition, we introduce the concept of 'Unverified Territory'. The teacher should sketch a simple division on the whiteboard: on one side is 'Our Intent' (what we want), and on the other side is 'The Executed Reality' (what actually runs on the computer). The AI occupies the space in between. Because AI models operate on statistical probability, they will confidently guess how to solve a problem even if they lack the correct tools or APIs to do so. This leads to the phenomenon of confident hallucinations. The teacher must explain that in software development, a single missing semicolon or a non-existent function name can halt an entire system. Therefore, every single line of code generated by an AI assistant must be treated as a hypothesis, not a fact, until it is systematically verified.

Next, the teacher walks through a concrete, illustrative scenario of an API hallucination on the whiteboard. Imagine asking the AI to 'integrate a modern weather forecast widget that fetches real-time data.' The AI, aiming to please, might generate code calling `WeatherAPI.fetchSuperAccurateForecast()`. This looks highly logical, but in reality, no such endpoint exists under that name. If the human simply copies and pasting this code, the system will crash immediately upon execution. The teacher will use this example to show how easily an unverified 'vibe' can lead to silent failures or immediate runtime errors. The core lesson here is that AI is an enthusiastic junior developer that needs boundaries, precise constraints, and constant verification.

This leads directly to the human checkpoint framework. The teacher should map out three critical checkpoints where the human must intervene. First, the 'Intent Check': does the AI's proposed plan actually match our goals? Second, the 'Signature Check': do the libraries, URLs, or external tools the AI suggests actually exist? Third, the 'Runtime Check': does the code run, and does it handle edge cases? By structuring these checkpoints, the teacher helps learners understand that vibe coding is not a single leap of faith, but a structured loop of prompt, generation, verification, and refinement.

To conclude the session, the teacher facilitates a guided analysis exercise. The class is presented with a scenario where an AI assistant generates code to send user notifications using a fake email library method called `Emailer.sendWithAutoRetry()`. The teacher guides the learners to identify where the integration would fail and asks them to formulate the exact follow-up prompt to correct the AI's assumption. This exercise is designed to reveal whether learners can spot the difference between syntactically correct code and semantically valid code, ensuring they leave the session ready to act as rigorous, proactive managers of their AI assistants.

tasks: Analyze a scenario where an AI assistant confidently hallucinates an API method, and identify how human check-points prevent integration failure.

sessions.title: Choosing a Beginner-Friendly Coding Environment
sessions.description: Compare zero-setup web-based environments (like Replit) with local setups (like Cursor/VS Code) to select the right tool for your learning curve.
sessions.sessionOutline:
To begin this lecture, the instructor should stand before a clean, empty whiteboard and draw a vertical line down the center, dividing it into two distinct zones. Label the left side 'The Cloud Sandbox' and the right side 'The Local Engine Room.' The goal of this opening beat is to shift the learner's perspective from traditional software configuration to selecting a 'canvas' for their ideas. Explain that in vibe coding, our primary constraint is not writing syntax, but maintaining a fast, uninterrupted feedback loop with our AI helper. The choice between a web-based environment and a local setup determines how much technical friction we must endure before we can see our ideas come to life.

On the left side of the board, the instructor will draw a self-contained bubble representing cloud platforms like Replit or StackBlitz. Inside this bubble, draw three interconnected icons: a code editor, a running server, and a live browser preview. Explain the concept of 'zero-setup' by using the analogy of a fully furnished, serviced apartment. The learner does not need to buy furniture, set up electricity, or fix the plumbing; they simply open a browser tab, and everything is instantly ready. This environment is highly visual and eliminates 'installation paralysis'—the common bottleneck where beginners give up because of terminal errors before they have even written their first line of code.

Transitioning to the right side of the board, the instructor will draw a computer chassis representing local environments like VS Code or Cursor. Here, sketch out separate, fragmented blocks: a local file system, a terminal window, and external software packages that must be downloaded manually. Use the analogy of a custom carpentry workshop. While this workshop is incredibly powerful, free to run forever, and fully customizable, the owner is solely responsible for sweeping the floors, setting up the tools, and troubleshooting broken machinery. For a beginner, managing local file paths, Node.js installations, or terminal environmental variables introduces a heavy cognitive load that can easily derail the creative flow of vibe coding.

Now, introduce the core framework for evaluating these two worlds through the lens of rapid prototyping. Explain that the main advantage of the cloud sandbox is speed-to-value: you can write a prompt, hit run, and share a working link with a friend in under five minutes. However, the trade-off is eventual cost and platform limitations. Conversely, local environments—especially AI-native IDEs like Cursor—offer unparalleled intelligence because the AI can index your entire computer's file system, providing deeply context-aware suggestions. The trade-off here is the setup cost in terms of human frustration when local configurations fail.

To wrap up the conceptual breakdown, address a common pitfall: the mistaken belief that cloud sandboxes are merely 'toys' and that 'real developers' must work locally. In the vibe coding era, professional developers routinely use cloud sandboxes to quickly isolate and test experimental prompts. To solidify this, conduct a brief whiteboard exercise. Draw three project scenarios on the board: a quick interactive calculator to show an investor, a personal website using standard templates, and a highly secure app processing private local files. Ask the audience to point to which side of the board each project belongs on, explaining that matching the tool to the immediate feedback requirement is the very first skill of a successful vibe coder.

tasks: Evaluate the pros and cons of local IDE setups versus cloud sandbox environments for a fast prototyping workflow.

sessions.title: Creating a New Project
sessions.description: Step-by-step walkthrough of starting a fresh workspace, explaining how template boilerplates are initialized.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by introducing the concept of a 'workspace' as a digital workbench. For absolute beginners, starting a project can feel like staring at a blank, intimidating canvas. The goal here is to demystify what actually happens when we press 'Create New Project' in an editor. Instead of viewing a new project as a complex system of configuration files, we explain that it is simply a designated, empty folder on a computer where we grant our AI assistant permission to read and write files. This shift in perspective transforms the workspace from a technical barrier into a safe playground.

Next, we walk through the mechanics of initializing a project workspace. Whether using a cloud sandbox like Replit or a local IDE setup, the process begins by creating a clean directory. We explain that many tools offer 'templates' or 'boilerplates'—pre-packaged bundles of basic files. We use a whiteboard analogy of a 'new house foundation': the template installs the basic framing (like a blank HTML structure and a basic stylesheet) so we don't have to build the literal studs of the house from scratch. We caution the educator to warn students against selecting overly complex templates (like full-stack React frameworks) at this stage. A simple static HTML/JS starter is always preferred to avoid 'dependency bloat' before we even write our first prompt.

Once the workspace is initialized, we guide students on how to prepare themselves to communicate with the AI assistant for the very first time. The common pitfall here is the 'magic wand' fallacy: expecting the AI to guess what they want with a single-sentence prompt like 'make a website'. We teach the concept of 'declaring intent'. Before typing any instructions, the student must define the scope of their project. We run through a quick interactive exercise where we write a mock introductory prompt on the board: establishing the role of the AI, outlining what we are trying to build, and defining the immediate, smallest next step. This prepares students to write intentional, iterative prompts that guide the AI step-by-step rather than asking for everything at once.

tasks: Set up a blank starter project directory and prepare to instruct the AI assistant for the very first time.

sessions.title: Understanding Files and Folders
sessions.description: Demystify standard project directories (HTML, CSS, JS, source folders) through high-level whiteboard visualizations.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Welcome back! Today we are diving into 'Understanding Files and Folders' using a highly visual, whiteboard-first approach designed for absolute beginners. In traditional coding, file structures feel like a dark labyrinth. In vibe coding, understanding this layout is your map. If you do not know how your project's files connect, you will not know what to ask the AI to change, and you will easily get lost when the AI generates code across multiple files. We will strip away the jargon and build a clear, intuitive mental model of a web application's anatomy.

Let's start by drawing a simple analogy on our physical or digital whiteboard. Imagine building a house. We represent this house using three core elements, which we draw as distinct boxes: a blueprint, a design board, and a power generator. In web development, these correspond to the three pillars of frontend code: index.html (the blueprint/skeleton), style.css (the paint/styling), and script.js (the mechanical wiring/interactivity). On the board, draw 'index.html' as a large box in the center, and place 'style.css' and 'script.js' on either side. 

The core logical chain starts with 'index.html'. This is the home base. Every web application begins here because web browsers are built to read HTML files first. On the whiteboard, draw a thick, solid arrow pointing from the browser window directly into index.html. Explain that this file defines what actually exists on the page—buttons, text boxes, and images—but does not determine how pretty they look or what happens when you click them. It is just the bare bones.

Now, how do these files talk to each other? This is where many beginners trip up. They think the computer magically knows to apply the styling and scripts just because the files live in the same directory. To prevent this misconception, draw explicit bridging lines on the board. From inside the `<head>` tag of our HTML box, draw an arrow pointing directly to 'style.css'. This represents the `<link>` tag—the visual bridge. Next, draw an arrow from just before the closing `</body>` tag of our HTML box pointing to 'script.js'. This represents the `<script>` tag—the functional bridge. Explain that index.html is the boss that actively imports and coordinates these external specialists.

Let's put this into practice with a brief mental mapping exercise. Ask the learners to sketch their own diagram of a simple app, like a digital kitchen timer. They should draw three boxes, label them with the appropriate file names, and draw the connection arrows. The goal of this exercise is to reveal if they understand which file handles which responsibility. If they try to write code that calculates the countdown time inside 'index.html', or put button styling in 'script.js', they will immediately catch their mistake by looking at their connection lines. 

Finally, we scale this up on our whiteboard to look at a typical folder hierarchy. Draw a root folder containing these three files, and introduce the concept of subfolders like '/assets' for images. Explain that when the AI proposes creating new files, the student must ensure the AI references the correct paths. If the AI places an image in '/assets/logo.png', our index.html needs to look inside that exact folder. By mastering this simple visual skeleton, learners transition from feeling overwhelmed by code folders to confidently managing their application's structure alongside their AI coding companion.

tasks: Draw a mental map representing how an index.html file connects with style.css and script.js files.

sessions.title: Running and Previewing an Application
sessions.description: Learn how the local or sandboxed server operates, allowing you to instantly preview changes in a web browser as they generate.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Welcome back, future vibe coders. In this session, we will demystify what actually happens when you press 'Run' or preview your application. For non-technical creators, the transition from looking at raw files to seeing a working website can feel like magic. Our goal today is to strip away the magic and replace it with a clear, conceptual understanding of how a local or sandboxed server operates, translating your code into a visual interface in real time.

Let's start our whiteboard explanation by drawing a simple diagram. On the left side, we have our workspace files—the index.html, style.css, and script.js files we structured in the previous session. On the right side, we have the web browser, which acts as the interpreter and canvas. In between them, we draw a bridge labeled 'The Development Server'. Beginners often make the mistake of thinking that web browsers can directly read files sitting on a hard drive like a word document. While technically possible for simple HTML, complex modern apps require a live 'server' to bundle, host, and serve these assets securely. Whether you are using a cloud-based environment like Replit or a local IDE with extensions, a micro-server is running in the background, listening for requests and delivering the updated files instantly.

Next, let's visualize the concept of 'Hot Reloading' or live previewing. Draw an arrow looping from the file workspace, through the dev server, and into the browser window. When you modify your code, the development environment detects the file change, automatically pushes the updates through the server, and triggers the browser to refresh without you having to manually reload the page. This instantaneous feedback loop is the lifeblood of vibe coding. Because you are collaborating with an AI to write and test code iteratively, being able to see visual updates within seconds allows you to evaluate and adapt your 'vibe' dynamically.

Now, let's address a common point of confusion: the preview port. When your server starts up, it opens a specific, secure digital doorway on your machine or sandboxed container, usually represented by an address like 'localhost:3000' or a custom preview URL. Explain this to students using the analogy of an apartment building: the IP address or host is the building's street address, while the port number is the specific apartment number where your app is currently hosting its party. If you try to open the browser but haven't started the server, or if you are looking at the wrong port, you will get a frustrating 'site cannot be reached' error. Demystifying this error early prevents students from thinking their code is broken when, in reality, the door to the apartment is simply closed.

We will wrap up this session with a hands-on verification exercise. Instruct students to launch their workspace's server, locate the active preview port, and open the rendered page. They will verify that their simple 'Hello World' page is rendering correctly. If they see the text displayed in the browser, the bridge is successfully built. This exercise teaches them to verify their execution environment first, establishing a rock-solid, predictable feedback loop before they begin prompting the AI to write more complex code.

tasks: Start your development environment's preview port and confirm your 'Hello World' page is rendering correctly.

sessions.title: Identifying the Problem
sessions.description: Pinpoint a clear, practical, and localized problem that a simple web application can solve effectively.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Welcome to the starting line of your building journey. As we step into the world of vibe coding, the absolute first superpower you must develop isn't writing prompts—it is choosing the right battle. In this session, we establish why the success of an AI-assisted project is decided before a single line of code is generated. When coding with natural language, your primary role shifts from 'syntax writer' to 'architect of intent'. If your intent is fuzzy, the AI's output will be a chaotic storm of features that quickly becomes impossible to debug. We begin by visualizing a simple truth on the whiteboard: the size of the problem you attempt to solve is inversely proportional to your likelihood of finishing it. 

To build intuition, the instructor will draw a large, messy circle labeled 'The Everything App' and contrast it with a tiny, razor-sharp point labeled 'The Localized Friction'. The core concept here is 'problem localization'. Students often fail because they try to clone complex platforms like Airbnb or Spotify on day one. Instead, we teach them to look for micro-frictions in their daily lives or immediate workflows—such as forgetting which plant was watered when, or losing track of daily micro-expenses. This localized focus ensures the code footprint remains small, the logic remains clean, and the AI can generate working code in a single, predictable pass.

Next, the instructor will break down the anatomy of a perfect, single-sentence problem statement. It must contain three components: the specific user, the exact moment of friction, and the negative impact of that friction. For example, instead of saying 'I want to build a fitness app,' we frame it as: 'Busy remote workers struggle to track their daily stretching intervals during back-to-back meetings, leading to physical fatigue.' This level of specificity acts as an anchor for the AI. It prevents scope creep and tells the LLM exactly what context to prioritize when it begins suggesting code structures.

To cement this understanding, we pivot to a live diagnostic exercise. The instructor will present common 'trap' statements on the board—such as 'I need an app with a database to track my books'—and show how these statements mistakenly jump straight to the solution instead of defining the problem. We will dissect why mentioning technical elements like 'databases' or 'cloud storage' at this stage actually restricts the AI's creative problem-solving. The session wraps up with students formulating their own single-sentence problem statements, focusing purely on human friction, which prepares them perfectly to establish boundaries for their Minimum Viable Product in the next session.

tasks: Formulate a single-sentence problem statement for a target application (e.g., 'A customized tracker for plant watering intervals').

sessions.title: Defining the User and Desired Outcome
sessions.description: Create a rudimentary user profile and outline exactly what operations they must be able to perform in the application interface.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by reframing how we approach software design when partnering with AI. The temptation in vibe coding is to jump straight into generating code without understanding who is using it. On the whiteboard, draw a stick figure next to a giant question mark, and explain that code exists only to bridge the gap between a human's current state and their desired outcome. If we do not define this human element, the AI will make assumptions for us, leading to a bloated, confusing user interface. By establishing clear user profiles, we give the AI a north star for design, usability, and functional requirements. This concept-first approach prevents us from building technically perfect software that solves the wrong human problem.

Next, introduce the classic User Story framework on the whiteboard, breaking it down into three simple components: Who, What, and Why. Draw three interconnected gears labeled 'Who is the person?', 'What action must they take?', and 'Why does it matter to them?'. Explain that the 'Who' defines the constraints (e.g., a busy parent has different attention span and device preferences than a professional developer). The 'What' is the specific interface action, and the 'Why' is the emotional or practical payoff. Emphasize that the 'Why' is the most critical element; it helps the AI understand the underlying motivation, which allows it to suggest better UI layouts and workflows that we might not have explicitly requested.

To cement this, walk through a concrete example of a plant-watering tracker. Contrast a poor, generic instruction like 'create a plant tracker' with a structured user scenario: 'As an forgetful apartment gardener, I want to log a plant's watering date with a single tap, so that I don't accidentally overwater it.' Point out how this single sentence tells the AI exactly what UI elements are needed—a fast tap button and a clear status display—and what to prioritize. This prevents the common trap of feature creep, where beginners try to design for everyone and end up with an unmanageable mess of inputs that confuses both the user and the AI code generator.

Transition to the interactive practice phase. Instruct learners to draft three diverse user scenarios for their target application. The goal here is not to create complex engineering documents, but to build empathy and boundaries. Guide them to select three different angles or edge-case users for their core concept. While they draft, watch out for the 'everything-bucket' pitfall, where a single scenario lists five different features at once. Remind them that each scenario should focus on one clean, isolated action. This isolation is crucial because we will feed these scenarios directly into the AI in the next unit to construct clean, modular application components.

tasks: Draft three basic user scenarios specifying 'who' uses the app, 'what' action they perform, and 'why' it brings value.

sessions.title: Limiting the First Version
sessions.description: Avoid scope creep by slicing requirements down to a Minimum Viable Product (MVP) that is quick to build and modify.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by introducing a metaphor that resonates deeply with non-technical creators: the difference between designing a multi-course banquet and baking a single, perfect loaf of bread. In vibe coding, beginners often fall into the trap of 'feature creep'—asking the AI to build authentication, real-time databases, custom themes, and payment processing all in their very first prompt. This structural overload inevitably leads to AI hallucination, broken code blocks, and a sense of defeat. The core objective of this session is to teach learners how to aggressively prune their app ideas into a Minimum Viable Product (MVP) that can be generated, tested, and understood within a single afternoon.

To visualize this concept, the teacher should draw a simple pyramid on the whiteboard. At the wide base is the 'Core Value Proposition'—the absolute minimum utility that solves the problem identified in Session 2.1.1. Above that are 'Nice-to-Haves' (like custom color schemes and history logs), and at the very top are 'Future Integrations' (like user logins and payment systems). The teacher will explain that for V1, we are slicing off everything except the base. The logic here is vital: every line of code the AI writes is a line of code the student may eventually need to troubleshoot. By keeping the codebase small, we keep the student's cognitive load low and guarantee a successful zero-to-one compilation loop.

A common mistake students make is believing that a simpler application is 'unimpressive.' The teacher should preemptively address this misconception by demonstrating how a highly focused, single-purpose tool that works flawlessly is infinitely more satisfying than a complex, multi-page app riddled with broken links. We illustrate this with a contrasting pair of scenarios: a giant 'Fitness Hub' app that crashes immediately upon loading vs. a simple 'Water Intake Reminder' button that instantly plays a sound and saves a tally to local browser storage. The latter represents a clean, fully functional V1 win that builds crucial momentum.

To ground this theory, we transition into an interactive whiteboard pruning exercise. The teacher will write a hypothetical feature list on the board for a 'Personal Plant Care Assistant.' The list includes: 1) A daily watering checklist, 2) A photo upload feature to identify plant diseases, 3) Push notifications, and 4) A community forum for plant owners. The teacher will then guide the audience through a logical elimination process. Why is photo disease identification a bad fit for V1? Because it requires complex external APIs and image processing. Why can we skip push notifications? Because they require background service workers and OS-level permissions. We physically cross these out on the board, leaving only the daily watering checklist as our robust, achievable V1.

Finally, the teacher will introduce the 'V1 Definition Test'—a self-evaluation rule of thumb. If a feature cannot be explained in a simple 'If I click X, Y happens' statement without involving words like 'database', 'account', or 'security', it does not belong in V1. This framework empowers learners to act as ruthless project managers of their own vibe coding journey, ensuring their first collaboration with AI remains focused, enjoyable, and ultimately successful.

tasks: Review a list of proposed features for your application and filter out anything that is non-essential for the core 'V1' launch.

lectures.title: Writing Effective Prompts
lectures.description: Master structured prompting strategies to extract predictable, clean, and bug-free code outcomes.

sessions.title: Describing the Project Clearly
sessions.description: Learn the mechanics of clear natural-language communication, avoiding vague directives that lead to generic code completions.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Welcome students by introducing a fundamental paradox of Vibe Coding: while we code using natural language and 'vibes,' the AI cannot read our minds. Absolute beginners often fall into the trap of treating the AI as an all-knowing wizard, typing vague commands and hoping for magic. On the whiteboard, draw a stick figure passenger telling a driver, 'Take me somewhere cool.' The driver is confused. Explain that without explicit direction, the AI will make assumptions to fill in the blanks, which often results in generic, bloated, or outright buggy code. The goal of this session is to establish the mindset of an active director rather than a passive spectator, teaching students how to articulate their project vision clearly using natural language.

Introduce the concept of 'Anatomy of a Project Description' on the whiteboard. Explain that a clean prompt is built on three core pillars: the Core Purpose, the User Experience (UX) Flow, and the Visual/Structural Layout. Use a flow diagram to show how a clear description acts as a blueprint. If we outline how a user enters the app, what they click, and how the app responds, the AI can construct a precise logical path. Walk through the logic chain: clarity in input yields modularity in output. When the AI doesn't have to guess the workflow, it writes isolated, clean functions instead of trying to build everything inside a single, chaotic block of code.

Now, tackle the classic anti-pattern: 'Make a calculator.' Write this phrase in red on the whiteboard. Ask the audience to consider what the AI assumes when it reads this. Does it build a simple 4-function calculator? A scientific calculator? A mortgage calculator? Show how this lack of clarity forces the model to fall back on its training data's statistical averages. This usually means it will generate a bare-bones, ugly HTML file with inline styles and basic alert boxes for answers. Explain that this is where most beginners get discouraged—not because the AI is bad, but because the instruction lacked a defined scope.

Transition into an interactive 'Prompt Upgrade' workshop on the board. Create a split screen: 'The Wish' on the left and 'The Blueprint' on the right. Step-by-step, rewrite 'Make a calculator' into a structured prompt. Show how to specify: 'Create a single-page web calculator designed for budgeting. It should have large, accessible buttons for addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division. Above the keypad, display a clear, real-time input history line and a main result display.' Explain to the instructor to highlight how we didn't use a single line of code, yet we have completely constrained the AI's creative freedom to align with our specific intent.

Conclude the session by addressing a major beginner misconception: the fear of not being 'technical' enough. Warn teachers that students often overcompensate by trying to use pseudo-code or half-understood programming jargon they copy-pasted, which actually confuses the AI. Reiterate that the true superpower of a vibe coder is logical clear-thinking in plain English. Wrap up with a visual summary showing how structured project descriptions save hours of debugging by getting the foundation right on the very first try.

tasks: Transform a vague prompt ('make a calculator') into a highly detailed and clear descriptive prompt.

sessions.title: Providing Context
sessions.description: Understand how to feed existing project constraints, technical parameters, and stack options to the AI model to establish scope boundaries.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this whiteboard session by establishing the concept of an AI's 'memory horizon' and why it is critical when building software. Without explicit context, an AI model behaves like a temporary worker who is dropped into an office with total amnesia, guessing what tools and files are available. To visualize this, the teacher should draw a bounded box on the physical or digital whiteboard labeled 'The Project Sandbox'. Inside this box, we sketch three distinct pillars: the Tech Stack (our tools), the File Tree (our existing assets), and the Environment Limitations (the rules of our playground). By establishing these boundaries early in a prompt, we prevent the AI from generating code that depends on libraries we don't have installed, or proposing architectures that don't fit our setup.

Next, the teacher will write out a live comparison on the board, demonstrating a 'blind prompt' versus a 'context-rich preamble'. The blind prompt is typically something like: 'Add a save button to my app.' The teacher will explain why this is a recipe for disaster: the AI will assume a random file structure, perhaps write in React when the user is using vanilla HTML, or assume a database is already hooked up. Directly next to this, the teacher drafts the anatomy of a perfect Context Preamble. This preamble introduces the project folder structure (e.g., showing a simple root folder containing index.html, style.css, and app.js) and explicitly states that we are running a local, no-build environment. This visual contrast immediately helps learners realize that context-setting is not about writing code; it is about setting the physical boundaries of the canvas before the paint is applied.

To solidify this, the teacher will guide learners through a hands-on exercise on the whiteboard: constructing a custom context preamble. We present a scenario where we have a very simple web application with just two files (index.html and main.js) and no external frameworks. The teacher will ask the students to draft a paragraph that explicitly tells the AI what files exist, what language version is being used, and what libraries are strictly forbidden. The core trap here is that beginners often forget to declare their 'no-build' status, causing the AI to import complex packages like Tailwind or npm modules that require a terminal-heavy setup. The teacher will point out how to preemptively shut down these hallucinations by inserting a strict 'Technical Constraints' section within the preamble.

We conclude the session by teaching the students how to maintain this context over a long chat session. The teacher illustrates how an AI's memory degrades over time, metaphorically showing how the 'Sandbox' walls can leak if we do not periodically remind the AI of the initial context or pin it to our system prompts. By the end of this session, students will transition from treating the AI as a magic mind-reader to treating it as an extremely competent contractor who simply needs a clear, structured brief about the construction site they are entering.

tasks: Write a context-setting preamble that informs the AI about the project's layout, environment limitations, and current file assets.

sessions.title: Setting Requirements and Constraints
sessions.description: Examine how to enforce explicit design constraints, architectural boundaries, and performance rules using positive and negative rules.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by addressing the 'eager-to-please' nature of LLMs, which is one of the most common pitfalls for absolute beginners. Explain that when an AI is asked to build a simple interactive element, its default behavior is to show off by pulling in modern frameworks, external libraries, and complex architectures that the user did not ask for and cannot easily debug. As a vibe coder, your job is not just to describe what you want, but to build a digital fence around the code. This session establishes how to build that fence using structured rules.

On the whiteboard, draw a large box representing your project container. Outside the box, write labels like 'Tailwind CDN', 'React', 'External APIs', and 'Complex Database'. Inside the box, draw a small, self-contained gear labeled 'Our Widget'. Explain to the audience that without constraints, the AI will build lines connecting your small widget to all those massive external blocks, making the code incredibly brittle. Show how 'Positive Rules' act as tracks guiding the AI's internal logic, while 'Negative Rules' act as physical shields that block external dependencies from leaking in.

Break down the anatomy of Positive Rules. These are instructions on architectural boundaries and data flow. For a beginner, the golden rule is simplicity. Teach the instructor to emphasize constraints such as 'Keep all HTML, CSS, and JS in a single file' or 'Store all application state in a single JavaScript object.' Explain the underlying logic: when all data is in one predictable spot, it is infinitely easier to ask the AI to inspect, fix, or modify it later. If the AI spreads state across five different places, a non-technical creator will quickly lose control of the application's behavior.

Transition to Negative Rules, which are often overlooked but carry immense power. Instructors should demonstrate how the AI defaults to using popular external assets—like Google Fonts or FontAwesome icons—which can break if the user is offline or if CDN links expire. Introduce the concept of strict vetoes: 'Do not use external icon libraries; use standard emojis instead,' or 'Do not use external CSS frameworks.' Explain that being explicit about what the AI *must not* do prevents it from making assumptions based on generic training data.

Introduce the practice exercise by framing it as a design challenge. Walk through drafting constraints for an interactive widget, such as a 'Vibe Journal'. Guide the students through converting a loose instruction into a bulleted boundary checklist: specifying zero external dependencies, local variable storage only, and single-file scope. Warn them about the trap of 'Constraint Suffocation'—giving contradictory rules that paralyze the AI. Conclude by illustrating how a well-constrained prompt guarantees code that is clean, highly readable, and exceptionally easy to debug, setting the stage for smooth development.

tasks: Draft a list of constraints for an interactive widget (e.g., 'must not use external frameworks, must store data in local variable only').

sessions.title: Providing Examples and References
sessions.description: Explore 'few-shot prompting' by feeding target examples, UI components, or standard templates to steer the model’s layout structure.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by addressing a classic limitation of natural language: the translation gap between human intention and structured code. In a public lecture style, the teacher starts on the whiteboard by drawing two columns: 'The Description' versus 'The Blueprint.' Under 'The Description,' we write a loose instruction like 'make a profile page with user stats.' Under 'The Blueprint,' we draw a concrete, minimal template of what we actually expect. The core teaching moment here is explaining that AI models are essentially pattern-matching engines; they perform exponentially better when shown a target structure rather than just a list of instructions. This is what prompt engineers call 'few-shot prompting,' and in vibe coding, it is the difference between an AI guessing your design and an AI instantly aligning with your precise data format.

Next, the teacher introduces the anatomy of a 'reference block' on the whiteboard. We draw a visual box labeled 'Reference Area' and show how to use markdown formatting (such as triple backticks) to cleanly segregate reference data from active instructions. The logical flow moves from setting the stage to defining the exact shape of information. We explain that when we want an AI to output complex data—such as a list of interactive cards or user profiles—giving it a physical template of the output JSON schema prevents it from making up random keys or nesting data in ways our application cannot read. The teacher explains the 'why' behind this: if the AI knows the precise shape of the puzzle piece, it can write the correct logic to handle that piece on the very first try without an iterative feedback loop of error-debugging.

To bridge this concept into practice, the teacher walks through a live construction of a mock JSON schema on the board. We start with a simple task: building a weather dashboard widget. Instead of letting the AI decide how to organize the weather metrics, we draft a simple JSON object on the whiteboard containing keys like 'temperature,' 'windSpeed,' and 'condition.' The teacher highlights a common pitfall: absolute beginners often assume the AI will only use the literal values provided in the example. We must explicitly instruct the teacher to guide students to add a meta-instruction like 'Use this JSON structure as a structural blueprint, but populate it with dynamic real-world values.' This prevents the AI from copying the mock data verbatim and instead teaches it to respect the structure while generating new logic.

Finally, the session transitions into the practice phase. The teacher challenges the class to draft their own reference block for a task tracker. This active learning moment is designed to reveal whether students can distinguish between the 'content' of an application and its 'structure.' If students struggle, the teacher steps in to demonstrate how a simple reference block acts as an anchor, ensuring that even if the 'vibe' of the conversation changes, the underlying data foundation remains rock-solid and predictable.

tasks: Create a reference block containing mock target JSON schemas to guide the AI's data formatting behavior.

lectures.title: Planning Before Generating Code
lectures.description: Ensure long-term project viability by requiring the AI assistant to formulate a blueprint prior to code output.

sessions.title: Asking AI to Propose a Plan
sessions.description: Instruct the AI to map out architectural steps, state-management paths, and styling workflows before writing a single line of application code.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by introducing a fundamental shift in the developer mindset, especially critical in the era of 'vibe coding': the transition from an immediate coder to a systems architect. In traditional development, jumping straight into typing code is a known recipe for messy architecture. In AI-assisted development, letting the AI generate lines of code immediately is even more dangerous, often resulting in a bloated 'black box' that the learner cannot manage. To illustrate this on the whiteboard, the instructor should draw a contrasting split-screen. On one side, show a chaotic pile of bricks representing 'immediate code generation,' which quickly collapses under its own weight. On the other side, sketch a clean, modular blueprint representing the 'plan-first approach.' This visual anchor helps learners appreciate that a plan is not a waste of time, but a mechanism for keeping the codebase clean, understandable, and modular from day one.

Next, we dive into the specific communication strategies required to force the AI into this 'planning mode.' The core challenge here is that AI models are naturally biased toward pleasing the user immediately, which often means dumping hundreds of lines of code at the first mention of a project. To prevent this, the instructor will demonstrate how to construct an explicit boundary prompt. On the whiteboard, write out the key components of a planning prompt: the Context, the Role (treating the AI as a Principal Software Architect), the Explicit Restriction ('Do not write any application code yet'), and the Deliverable ('Provide a high-level step-by-step implementation plan including state management, UI structure, and external data flow'). The instructor should emphasize why the explicit restriction is the most critical line; without it, the model's default behavior will override the request for a plan.

To solidify this, the instructor will walk through a common pitfall: the 'compliance slip,' where the AI acknowledges the request for a plan but sneaks code into the response anyway. Teachers should explain to learners that if this happens, they must not accept the code. Instead, they should reply with a corrective prompt, reminding the AI of its role as an architect. We want to teach learners that managing an AI is like managing a junior developer who is eager to code but needs structure. The logic chain flows from establishing authority, defining the boundary, and enforcing compliance before a single line of CSS or JavaScript is written.

Finally, we engage the classroom with an interactive prompt-building exercise. The instructor presents a scenario, such as wanting to build a simple interactive habit tracker. Instead of writing the tracker, students are asked to draft the exact prompt they would send to the AI to get *only* a blueprint. The instructor will evaluate these student responses on the whiteboard, highlighting prompt elements that successfully restrain the AI versus those that leave loopholes for code dumping. This exercise reveals whether students have understood how to control the AI's output format, ensuring they are fully prepared to act as directors of their software projects rather than passive observers.

tasks: Construct a prompt that requests a step-by-step construction plan from an AI agent instead of instant code generation.

sessions.title: Reviewing the Proposed Plan
sessions.description: Inspect the AI's proposed design with a critical eye, verifying that the architectural approach aligns with simple and manageable coding frameworks.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by introducing the concept of the 'Vibe Critic.' In the traditional coding world, system architects review technical blueprints to ensure they are viable. In the vibe coding era, the human creator must act as this architect, even without a computer science degree. The teacher will draw a direct contrast on the whiteboard between an elegant, minimalist structure and an over-engineered 'tech stack monster.' The core idea here is that AI models are trained on massive enterprise codebases, meaning their default inclination is often to propose overly complex architectures—such as recommending external databases, heavy state-management libraries, or cloud infrastructure—when a simple, local client-side script would easily suffice for a Minimum Viable Product (MVP). By learning to spot these complexities early, students prevent their projects from collapsing under the weight of unneeded dependencies before they even begin.

Next, the teacher will sketch out a 'Complexity Red Flag Checklist' on the whiteboard to help students categorize different parts of an AI's proposal. We categorize these red flags into three main areas: unnecessary external dependencies (like importing heavy framework wrappers), premature backend infrastructure (such as requesting a PostgreSQL database instead of browser-based LocalStorage), and overly complex data flows (like using state management libraries for a three-step form). The teacher should walk through the logic of why each flag is dangerous: more moving parts mean more points of failure, making debugging extremely difficult when things inevitably go wrong. The goal is to cultivate an eye for simplicity, encouraging learners to ask the AI: 'Can we build this using only vanilla frontend tools first?'

To solidify this mindset, the teacher will present an interactive exercise on the whiteboard by displaying a real-world scenario: building a simple digital grocery list. The teacher will write out a mock AI proposal that includes a Node.js backend, a MongoDB database setup, and complex routing. The teacher will then guide the class in a 'spot-the-bloat' interactive run, physically circling the components that are too complex for a beginner MVP and crossing them out, replacing them with simple browser-native alternatives like simple JS arrays and local storage. This interactive diagnostic prevents the common beginner mistake of assuming that a longer, more complex AI proposal is inherently better or more 'professional.'

We wrap up the session by demonstrating how to write a refinement prompt that forces the AI to simplify its plan. The teacher writes a template on the board: 'This is too complex. Strip out all databases and servers. Rewrite the plan using only a single HTML file, local CSS, and plain JavaScript, storing all data in the browser memory.' This establishes the critical transition from passive consumer of AI outputs to an active supervisor, setting the stage for breaking this simplified, clean plan down into sequential micro-tasks in the next session.

tasks: Analyze an AI-generated architecture plan and flag areas that are unnecessarily complex for a beginner MVP.

sessions.title: Dividing the Plan into Small Tasks
sessions.description: Break a broad developmental blueprint into sequential micro-tasks to respect AI context limits and maintain clear, structured debugging.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by introducing a fundamental constraint of working with Large Language Models: the concept of context drift and cognitive overload. To make this abstract concept tangible on our whiteboard, draw a physical funnel representing the AI's 'attention span'. Explain that while an AI can generate a grand blueprint for an entire application, asking it to execute that entire blueprint in a single prompt is like asking a builder to construct a whole house in a single day without intermediate inspections. The result is inevitably missing doors, misaligned plumbing, and structurally weak code. The core lesson here is that in 'Vibe Coding', our role shifts from writer to supervisor, and a supervisor's chief duty is assigning bite-sized, sequential tasks.

Next, visually map out the 'Micro-Task Pipeline' on the whiteboard. Contrast two approaches: the 'Big Bang' approach (one giant prompt containing layout, logic, styling, and validation) versus the 'Layered' approach. Sketch the Layered approach as a staircase. Step one is always the static structural skeleton—the bare layout without logic or beauty. Step two introduces basic interactivity, like capturing user input. Step three layers on validation and edge cases, and step four applies the visual design and styling. Explain the underlying engineering logic of this staircase: by isolating variables, if the application breaks, we instantly know which layer is responsible. If the form stops submitting during step three, we do not need to debug the CSS from step four.

Address a critical misconception that beginners often fall into: the 'efficiency trap'. Many learners assume that writing one long prompt saves time, or they worry that breaking it up will make the AI 'forget' the overall goal. On the whiteboard, demonstrate how to construct a 'Context Bridge'. This is a technique where each sequential prompt explicitly references the progress made so far and references the master plan established in the previous session. Teach the instructor to model this phrasing explicitly, showing how a prompt like 'Now that we have the HTML structure from Step 1, let's implement the input validation' keeps the AI anchored without triggering context degradation.

Conclude the session with a practical, interactive deconstruction exercise. Walk the students through a scenario: building a simple 'Habit Tracker'. On the whiteboard, list the chaotic, unorganized features a beginner might want to build all at once. Step-by-step, guide the audience in restructuring this chaotic list into a clean, sequential checklist of four distinct, promptable tasks. Show how each step yields a testable micro-prototype. This exercise is designed to reveal the psychological shift required for successful Vibe Coding—learning to resist the urge to rush to the final aesthetic and instead mastering the discipline of incremental, stable progress.

tasks: Deconstruct an overall feature plan into a checklist of isolated, sequential prompts (e.g., UI layout first, then validation logic, then styling).

projects.stage_description: Formulate a clear prompt requesting a core design blueprint and a phased feature list for the Habit Tracker. Have the AI generate a logical execution plan and break it down into tiny, step-by-step development tasks.
projects.deliverable_increment: A 'planning.md' file inside your repository detailing the system architecture, component checklist, and phase-by-phase implementation schedule approved by the AI.
