units.title: Building a First Application
units.description: Transition from plans to live structures. Instruct the AI assistant to assemble the core foundation of a web interface, style it beautifully, program deep functional interactivity, safely capture inputs, read and explain code patterns, and identify standard dependency footprints.

lectures.title: Creating the Application Foundation
lectures.description: Initialize the structural skeletal framework of your target MVP using natural language.

sessions.title: Generating the Starter Application
sessions.description: Prompt the AI to construct the primary folder organization, configuration files, and base template code.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Welcome to the first session of Unit 3, where we move from abstract planning to concrete creation. Today, we are focusing on generating the starter application foundation. For a non-technical creator, the absolute starting point of any codebase can feel like an impenetrable barrier. They might ask: 'What folders do I need?', 'What is a package.json or config file?', and 'How do I avoid breaking something before I even begin?' The goal of this session is to demystify this initial setup. By framing the project scaffolding not as 'code' but as the digital filing cabinet of their application, we transition the student's mental model from passive observer to active manager. We want to teach them that the skeleton of their application is simply a structured home where their ideas will live.

To make this concrete, imagine a whiteboard divided into two halves. On the left side, draw a simple blueprint of a physical house: foundation, walls, and utility hookups. On the right side, draw the corresponding software components: a root folder (the site/foundation), an index.html file (the layout/walls), and a configuration file (the utility meters). Explain to the students that when we prompt our AI assistant, we aren't just asking for 'some code'; we are instructing it to construct these precise, basic structural pillars. Introduce the concept of a 'Single-Page Application' (SPA) as a house that updates its internal rooms instantly without making the user step outside and walk through a new front door every time. This visualization addresses the common beginner misconception that every button click requires building a completely separate, heavy webpage.

Now, let's look at the instruction phase. Explain to the class that the most common pitfall when asking an AI to generate a starter template is lack of constraints, which leads the AI to make wild assumptions. It might write a complex Node.js server when a simple HTML/JS file would do, or it might introduce heavy frameworks that require local command-line tools to run. To prevent this, the teacher should model a 'Skeletal Prompt'. This prompt must explicitly declare: 'Create a single-page web application using only vanilla HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Keep it contained in a single index.html file or a clean three-file folder structure (index.html, styles.css, app.js). No external build tools or installations are allowed.' By using this exact phrasing, we ensure the starter template is error-free, lightweight, and immediately openable in any browser.

At this point, introduce an interactive practice moment. Ask the students to draft a prompt for their virtual AI assistant to initialize their desired application. As they write, have them identify which words in their instructions prevent the AI from generating unnecessarily bloated code. Warn them about the 'dependency trap'—when the AI suggests importing third-party libraries (like React or Tailwind via complex build chains) too early. Instead, teach them to guide the AI to use simple CDN links if external styling is absolutely necessary. This teaches the students to treat the AI as a junior builder who needs strict, clean boundaries.

We conclude this session by simulating the generated output on our whiteboard. Show how the AI outputs a clean, well-commented directory structure alongside a standard, valid HTML boilerplate containing `<head>`, `<body>`, and placeholder links. Point out that the initial code is deliberately simple. This simplicity is not a failure; it is a clean canvas. Explain that starting with a minimal, working, and error-free base is a software engineering best practice. It ensures that when we add features in the next sessions, we will know exactly what broke if an error occurs. In the next session, we will begin sketching inside these digital walls by defining our interface's layout zones.

tasks: Instruct the AI assistant to assemble a basic, error-free starter template for a single-page web app.

sessions.title: Creating the Page Structure
sessions.description: Define logical zones of your interface (header, form dashboard, content feed) and direct the AI to produce clear structural components.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by addressing a common trap beginner 'vibe coders' fall into: asking the AI to 'build a dashboard' or 'make a landing page' without first establishing the spatial layout. When students jump straight to requesting a completed interface, the AI is forced to make assumptions, often resulting in a messy, unstructured wall of elements. To prevent this, the teacher must introduce the conceptual metaphor of 'the wireframe wire-up' using a digital whiteboard. By drawing simple boxes to represent distinct spatial areas—such as a header, a side-by-side dashboard layout, and a scrollable content feed—we teach students that code structure is simply a nested set of boxes. This visual mental model is crucial because it helps non-technical creators realize that they do not need to understand HTML tags; they only need to understand spatial relationships.

Moving deeper into the lesson, the teacher should guide students on how to translate these visual boxes into 'zones' using plain, structured English. For example, rather than telling the AI to 'write HTML', the student should learn to write a hierarchical markdown prompt that names each zone and describes its position. The teacher will sketch out a three-tier layout hierarchy on the board: a global header at the top, a main workspace divided into a left-side input form and a right-side visualizer, and a bottom status bar. We explain to the students that by defining these regions clearly in their instructions, the AI is guided to generate modular, easy-to-read code blocks that correspond directly to their mental model, preventing code spaghetti later on.

Next, the teacher will address a frequent mistake: confusing the layout zones with the content that goes inside them. To prevent students from overloading their structural prompts with specific text, labels, and behavior, the teacher should model a 'structure-first' prompt. We explain that in this phase, we only want the AI to frame the empty containers—like building the skeletal studs of a house before choosing the wallpaper. The teacher will demonstrate how a prompt like 'Create a layout with two columns: Column A on the left taking up 30% width, and Column B on the right taking up 70% width' acts as a scaffold that ensures the visual foundation is completely stable before any UI components are injected.

We conclude with an active reflection moment. The teacher presents a poorly worded, chaotic prompt that mixes design aesthetic, feature requests, and structure all in one sentence, and asks the students to point out where the layout structure is lost. Through this exercise, students learn to spot 'instruction clutter' and practice distilling a chaotic idea into clean layout zones. This builds the fundamental intuition needed to guide an AI assistant systematically, transforming the learner from a passive prompt-sender into a deliberate structural designer.

tasks: Map the layout zones of your target interface and write structural instructions to render them as structured sections.

sessions.title: Adding Content
sessions.description: Fill key page blocks with static headers, explanatory paragraphs, labels, and clean informational structures.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by addressing a common trap in 'vibe coding': trying to build fully dynamic features and complex state management before the user interface has any real substance. In a public-lecture format, the teacher must explain that building the visual and textual foundation of an application is like drawing a wireframe with real words. Before asking an LLM to wire up interactive buttons or database queries, students need to establish semantic headers, descriptive label texts, and mock content blocks. This gives both the human creator and the AI a physical 'anchor' in the code. It ensures that when we later ask the AI to make things interactive, it already knows exactly which UI element is supposed to change, rather than guessing or accidentally generating a completely different HTML layout. To visualize this concept, the teacher should draw a simple 'Content Skeleton' on the whiteboard. On one side, draw a generic box labeled 'Unstructured Text Container'. On the other, draw a clear visual hierarchy with an 'H1: Dashboard Title', 'H2: Section Header', descriptive helper text underneath, and specific input labels. The teacher should emphasize that using semantic content like standard headers (H1, H2, H3) and proper paragraph tags (

) isn't just about typography; it acts as a structural roadmap for the AI assistant. When we write prompts asking the AI to add realistic placeholder data or fill in specific text zones, having these clear semantic boundaries prevents the LLM from getting confused about where one component ends and another begins. Next, the teacher will walk through the technique of writing 'Directed Content Prompts'. Instead of giving a vague instruction like 'add some text to the page', a vibe coder should learn to specify the tone, length, and exact placement of the text. For example, the teacher can demonstrate a prompt like: 'In the main content zone, replace the generic text block with a clear H2 header reading "Your Daily Performance" and add three bullet points explaining key metrics using realistic mock data.' This shows learners how to direct the AI to populate layouts constructively. The teacher should highlight a critical mistake here: allowing the AI to generate long paragraphs of generic 'Lorem Ipsum' text. While standard in traditional web design, generic placeholder text makes it harder to evaluate if the application 'vibe' and functional purpose feel right. Using realistic, domain-specific mock text makes the development process feel concrete immediately. To consolidate this understanding, the session transitions into an active-learning moment. The teacher presents a poorly-structured, empty layout on the whiteboard and asks the students to draft a prompt that instructs an AI to insert a multi-step instructions banner at the top of the interface. The goal of this exercise is to reveal whether students can pinpoint exactly where the content should go (e.g., 'right below the main header') and specify the structural elements (e.g., 'an ordered list with three steps and bold prefixes'). The teacher will review common student drafts, pointing out how adding specific content-focused keywords prevents the AI from generating bloated, unstructured div soup and maintains a clean, understandable codebase that is ready for styling and interactivity in the next phases.

tasks: Refine the structural layout files with semantic headers and descriptive placeholder texts using directed prompts.

sessions.title: Adding Basic Visual Styling
sessions.description: Incorporate modern styling paradigms. Instruct the AI to construct clean visual presentation rules, colors, layouts, and typography styles.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Welcome back to our final session of Unit 3, where we shift our focus from functional structure to visual presentation. In a classic public lecture style, we will address styling not as writing line-by-line CSS rules, but as translating structural layouts into beautiful, modern aesthetics through human-in-the-loop 'Vibe Coding'. The goal today is to understand how we can guide our AI assistant to transition a raw, wireframed HTML application into a polished, responsive dark-mode layout with pristine visual typography. We start by conceptualizing how design systems work in a natural-language workflow, emphasizing that styling is not merely 'making things look pretty' but creating visual hierarchy that guides the user's attention.

To make this intuitive, we will use a whiteboard visualization. Picture our interface as a grid of containers. I want you to sketch a simple two-column layout on the board: a main dashboard on the left, and a contextual sidebar on the right. Traditionally, achieving this required understanding CSS Grid or Flexbox syntax, which often trips up beginners with complex alignment properties. Instead of writing that syntax, our teaching focus is on translating this mental layout into an aesthetic 'vibe prompt'. We explain to the AI what our columns are, how they should stack on smaller screens (like a mobile phone), and the emotional tone we want to set—in this case, a clean, distraction-free 'dark mode' featuring soft charcoal backgrounds, high-contrast neon accents, and clean sans-serif typography.

A major pitfall students encounter here is writing vague prompts like 'make it look modern.' Modern is subjective, and the AI might return an over-engineered stylesheet that is hard to debug or modify later. To prevent this, we teach students to use concrete visual references and constraints. We show them how to instruct the AI to use specific, clean design systems—such as tailwind-style utility classes or a single, self-contained CSS block—while keeping our underlying HTML semantic. We teach them to specify structural constraints, such as 'use a maximum content width of 1200px, center the application on the screen, and ensure all buttons have clear hover states with subtle transitions.' This guarantees that the AI generates responsive, predictable code rather than a chaotic mix of colors.

We will wrap up this session with an interactive practice moment. We will ask students to formulate a specific, descriptive prompt aimed at transforming their plain white application skeletal framework into a dark-mode layout. As they draft this, we want them to explicitly define three visual variables for the AI: the primary dark background color, the accent color for active elements, and the responsive breakpoint where the two-column layout collapses into a single vertical stack. This exercise is designed to reveal whether learners have grasped the connection between layout structure and visual instructions, preparing them to confidently direct the aesthetic evolution of any AI-assisted project.

tasks: Formulate styling instructions to achieve a clean, professional dark-mode design with responsive layout columns.

lectures.title: Adding Functionality
lectures.description: Transform static visual components into highly responsive, interactive application features.

sessions.title: Adding Buttons and User Actions
sessions.description: Direct the AI to intercept user interactions (clicks, keypresses) and establish interactive behavior.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by addressing the shift from static visual design to dynamic interaction. In a classic development setting, connecting a button to an action requires manually querying the DOM and binding event handlers. In a 'vibe coding' paradigm, the learner does not need to memorize syntax, but they absolutely must understand the conceptual bridge of 'listening' for user intent. The teacher should visualize this on the whiteboard as an 'ear' attached to a button, waiting for a specific physical action like a click or keypress, which then triggers a predefined reaction sequence. This high-level intuition helps students understand that software is not just an aesthetic layout, but a system of cause and effect.

To build this intuition, the teacher will draw a conceptual sequence diagram showing three steps: User Action (e.g., clicking a 'Submit' button), the Invisible Listener (the hook that detects the click), and the UI Reaction (e.g., a modal popping up or a color changing). Explaining this sequence is vital because absolute beginners often assume AI can read a user's mind; they must realize that every responsive element requires an explicit instruction for the AI to register the event. This sets up the logical flow for constructing the prompt: first, name the target element; second, define the trigger event; and third, detail the expected visual reaction.

A major pitfall at this stage is 'over-prompting'—asking the AI to add dozens of interactions all at once, which leads to broken script linkages and messy event bubbling. The teacher should actively warn against this, advising learners to address one interactive element at a time. For instance, the instructor will model how to draft a surgical prompt targeting just a single 'Like' button: instructing the AI to locate the button, listen for a click, and toggle its visual state from empty to filled. By keeping the scope small, the generated code remains easy to verify, and the learner can instantly see if the 'vibe' is working.

Finally, the teacher transition students into an active practice scenario. Students will write a prompt directing the AI to add an event listener to a primary action button on their mock UI, causing a confirmation toast or message to appear on screen. The goal of this exercise is to help students recognize that they must define not just the 'what' (the button), but the 'when' (on click) and the 'then' (the visual feedback). Through this, they learn to act as clear directors, guiding the AI to build reliable interactive logic without getting lost in the syntax of event listeners.

tasks: Prompt the AI to add event listeners to UI buttons that trigger interface feedback when clicked.

sessions.title: Accepting User Input
sessions.description: Implement form elements, sliders, and checkboxes, teaching the AI how to grab input safely without crashing the UI state.
sessions.sessionOutline:
This whiteboard session focuses on the critical gateway of any interactive application: receiving, validating, and managing user input. For a vibe coder, user input is historically a major source of application instability. Because AI models generated to look good often skip the 'boring' logic of handling edge cases, our main goal is to show how to direct the AI to handle form elements safely. We will use a whiteboard to visually break down the path of user input from the screen to the application's memory space, illustrating how unvalidated data can crash a UI state. By taking a concept-first public lecture style, we make this architectural boundary intuitive without getting bogged down in syntax.

We start by drawing a simple split diagram on the whiteboard: on the left, we draw a text input box and a numeric slider; on the right, we draw a fragile 'application core' holding the application's active state. Connecting them is an open pipe we label 'User Input'. Explain to the audience that in raw visual code, whatever a user types goes straight through this pipe. If the core expects a clean number like '5' to calculate a budget, but a user leaves the box empty or types 'hello', the arithmetic breaks, the application crashes, and the screen goes blank—a common vibe coding tragedy. The core takeaway here is that we must instruct the AI to build a 'gatekeeper' right at the entrance of that pipe.

To prevent the classic mistake of letting the AI write code that blindly trusts user data, the teacher will write a template prompt on the board. This prompt demonstrates how to demand defensive validation structures. We teach the audience to instruct the AI using natural language rules: 'Whenever the user clicks submit, first check if the input is empty or contains non-numeric characters. If it does, stop the execution and show a friendly red warning label near the input field instead of updating the application state.' By visualizing this validation loop as a simple flow chart—Input -> Validation Check -> (If Error: Show Help Label) -> (If clean: Update State)—the audience learns to design the logical safety nets that make AI-generated code resilient.

We wrap up the session with an interactive practice scenario where we challenge the audience to design a robust validation flow for a numeric input field, such as an age or budget calculator. The teacher will sketch out common edge cases on the board—such as negative numbers, astronomical values, or decimal points—and guide the audience on how to explicitly prompt the AI to catch these boundaries. This exercise shifts the learner's perspective from merely designing pretty UI forms to actively directing the AI to enforce safe, predictable, and clean data flows.

tasks: Build a validation flow with the AI to handle empty text fields or incorrect numeric inputs from form inputs.

sessions.title: Updating Information on the Screen
sessions.description: Instruct the AI to build dynamic reactivity, dynamically changing the screen content based on user interaction without a full page refresh.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this whiteboard session by introducing the concept of dynamic reactivity. In a concept-first public lecture style, we avoid diving straight into Javascript syntax or complex framework lifecycles. Instead, the teacher should draw a clear distinction on the whiteboard between static content—like a printed poster—and dynamic content, which behaves like a live dashboard. The core idea to establish early on is the 'data loop': a user performs an action, the application's internal data (or state) changes, and the screen automatically updates to reflect that new data without requiring a full page refresh. This is the heart of modern web application feeling 'snappy' and responsive, and helping learners conceptualize this cycle is crucial before they instruct an AI to write code for it.

Next, the teacher will illustrate a simple visual counter on the whiteboard to represent this 'state-to-view' mapping. On the left side of the board, sketch a box labeled 'State (Internal Memory)' containing a single variable, like `counter = 0`. On the right side, sketch the 'UI (User Interface)' showing a big, bold number '0'. Draw a double-headed arrow connecting them, showing how changes to the internal variable must instantly trigger an update on the screen. The teacher should highlight a common pitfall here: beginners often think that updating a variable in code automatically updates the text on the screen. The teacher needs to visually demonstrate that there is an explicit step where the developer (or the AI helper) must target the specific HTML element and rewrite its text content. Without this explicit step, the code has a 'silent update' bug where the internal math is correct but the user sees nothing change.

Moving to the hands-on practice scenario, the teacher guides learners on how to direct an AI model to implement this behavior safely. Rather than writing code manually, the student will write a conceptual prompt. The teacher should whiteboard a prompt structure that explicitly asks the AI to separate the 'state' from the 'rendering logic'. For example, instructing the AI to 'Create a counter variable, write a function that updates this variable when a button is clicked, and then call a separate render function that updates the DOM element text' helps prevent the AI from generating spaghetti code where state and UI updates are tangled together. This structured approach ensures that when the application grows, the code remains modular and easier to debug.

Finally, the teacher introduces a quick whiteboard exercise to test comprehension: ask the students how they would prompt the AI to change not just a number, but also a visual label's color based on that number (for example, making the text red when the count is negative and green when positive). This exercise is designed to reveal whether students understand that the visual presentation is a direct projection of the underlying data state. By teaching them to think in terms of state-driven UI, they learn to command AI coders with high-level architectural intent rather than getting lost in low-level code micro-management.

tasks: Establish an updated interface state counter that increments and changes visual labels instantly when inputs update.

sessions.title: Saving Information Locally
sessions.description: Utilize simple browser-side database protocols (LocalStorage) so that user information survives browser refreshes.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Welcome back to our series on Vibe Coding. In this public-lecture-style whiteboard session, we are going to demystify a crucial concept that elevates any simple project from a temporary 'vibey' prototype into a real-world tool: local persistence. Up until now, our application has been living entirely in the volatile, fleeting memory of the active browser tab. If a user hits refresh, or if their browser crashes, everything they have done vanishes. To build a robust prototype, we need our AI to implement a way to save data on the user's device. We will use a built-in web technology called 'LocalStorage'.

To visualize this, imagine a physical whiteboard split into two sections: the active workspace (volatile RAM) and a tiny personal locker built right into the browser wall (LocalStorage). When the page loads, the locker is checked; if there's anything inside, we pull it out and put it on the table. When the user types or updates their information, we immediately write a copy of that new state and slide it into the locker. This visual conceptualization is crucial because beginners often confuse saving data with complex server-side databases. By focusing on LocalStorage, we keep the stack simple, no-setup, and completely client-side, matching our concept-first public lecture approach.

Now, how do we direct the AI to handle this? This is where the magic of Vibe Coding comes in, but also where common pitfalls arise. A major trap is asking the AI simply to 'save my form data.' If we are too vague, the AI might generate complex, over-engineered code using backend technologies like Node.js or external databases, which completely breaks our lightweight local vibe. Instead, our whiteboard prompt should guide the AI with specific guardrails: 'I want to persist the form input values in the browser's LocalStorage. Please generate the code to automatically save these inputs whenever they change, and load them back into the form fields when the page is refreshed.'

To put this into action, we will run through a practice scenario on our virtual whiteboard. We'll simulate prompting the AI to write a sync helper. This exercise reveals a classic logical hurdle: state synchronization. Students often struggle to understand that saving is only half the battle; loading the saved data back into the UI when the page first loads is just as important. If the AI only writes the 'save' logic but misses the 'initial load' sequence, users will see empty forms even though the data is technically in their browser's storage. We will explicitly visualize this two-way flow on the whiteboard, showing the 'Save on Change' and 'Load on Start' loops, enabling learners to critically evaluate the code the AI returns and spot missing recovery logic before testing it.

tasks: Direct the AI to persist local form inputs into browser memory and successfully retrieve them when reloading the webpage.

lectures.title: Understanding the Generated Project
lectures.description: Peel back the layers of your generated files. Demystify code patterns to understand the logical flow of your application.

sessions.title: Finding the Main Project Files
sessions.description: Locate files that handle layout, styles, database storage, configuration, and background script executions.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Welcome to Session 3.3.1. In this session, we will demystify the structure of a modern software project generated by AI, using a whiteboard-style visualization to make files and folders intuitive. For a absolute beginner, opening an AI-generated codebase can feel like staring at a dense, alien city. They see directories like 'src', config files, style sheets, and distribution folders. Our primary goal is to help them map this digital terrain conceptually, transforming fear of the unknown into structure. This session adopts a 'concept-first public lecture' approach, ensuring that even without any coding background, students can immediately recognize where the skeleton, skin, and muscles of their application live.

We begin on our virtual whiteboard by drawing a simple analogy: building a house. Every house has raw materials that the builders use (source code), blueprints that guide the construction (configuration files), and the final, polished house that people actually move into (the build artifacts or production-ready files). In a typical modern project structure, we visualize this by drawing three distinct columns on the whiteboard. The first column is 'The Engine Room' (usually the `src` or source folder), where our primary logic and scripts live. The second column is 'The Wardrobe' (containing styling sheets like `styles.css`), which dictates how things look. The third column is 'The Command Center' (root files like configurations and manifests), which dictates how different systems connect. By visualizing these buckets, we prevent the common beginner pitfall of feeling overwhelmed by the sheer volume of files—most of them are just support staff for the main actors.

Next, the instructor should walk through how code moves from these source folders into the final preview they see in their browser. Many beginners get confused when they modify a file in a folder called 'dist' or 'build' and find their changes overwritten later. We must explicitly address this conceptual trap: 'dist' or 'build' folders are the 'baked cakes', while 'src' is the 'mixing bowl'. We teach learners that we only ever edit the ingredients in the mixing bowl (`src`). The AI or build tools will automatically bake them into the finished cake in the build folder. This distinction is critical because editing build artifacts directly is a highly common mistake that leads to lost work and immense frustration.

To solidify this, we introduce an active-learning checking point. The instructor draws a mock directory tree on the whiteboard, containing items like `index.html`, `src/main.js`, `styles/global.css`, `package.json`, and `dist/index.html`. We ask the students: 'If we want to change the color of our primary button, or if we want to change the behavior when that button is clicked, which files are we targeting?' We guide them to locate the stylesheets for layout and visual appearance, and the primary script entry points (like `main.js`) for behavior. This exercise ensures that before they even prompt an AI to write code, they know exactly which file the AI is referring to when it hands back a snippet of CSS or JavaScript.

tasks: Verify where your build artifacts, styling sheets, and primary script entry points reside in your project directory tree.

sessions.title: Asking AI to Explain Existing Code
sessions.description: Engage with your AI partner as a private tutor, asking it to annotate and deconstruct complex parts of your generated scripts.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by addressing the psychological trap of vibe coding: the temptation to treat generated code as a black box that 'just works' until it suddenly does not. Explain to the instructors that the goal of this session is to transform the student from a passive copy-paster into an active, questioning director. On the whiteboard, draw a large magnifying glass focusing on a block of abstract code symbols. This visualization represents the shift from high-level vibes to micro-level understanding. Emphasize that the AI is not just a code generator but a patient, infinite-resource tutor capable of explaining its own output at any level of abstraction.

Introduce the concept of 'prompt zooming' to help students navigate different depths of code understanding. On the whiteboard, illustrate this as a three-tier ladder: the top tier is 'The Bird's Eye View' (what does this file do conceptually?), the middle tier is 'The Blueprint' (how do these functions connect?), and the bottom tier is 'The Microscope' (what does this exact line mean?). Instructors should model how to formulate prompts for each level. For instance, show how asking 'Explain this like I am a chef' or 'Translate this JavaScript logic into plain English' can strip away intimidating syntax and reveal the underlying logic.

Demonstrate a live 'interrogation' of an AI-generated script. Use a common but confusing snippet on the board, such as an event listener or a state updating function. Walk through the process of highlighting this exact snippet and writing an structured interrogation prompt. Teach the students to ask specific follow-up questions like 'What is the purpose of this parameter?', 'What happens if this input is empty?', and 'Why did you use this method instead of a simpler loop?'. This prevents the AI from generating generic summaries and forces it to provide targeted, logical breakdowns.

Address a critical learner pitfall: the 'illusion of competence.' When an AI explains code smoothly, students often nod along and assume they understand it, only to find they cannot modify or troubleshoot it later. To counter this, introduce the 'Reverse Teach-Back' technique. Instructors should demonstrate how a student can explain their own understanding of the code back to the AI and ask, 'Did I understand this correctly? What edge cases did my explanation miss?'. This active feedback loop anchors the concepts and builds genuine technical intuition.

Conclude by guiding the students through their hands-on practice. Instruct them to select a piece of code from their current project that feels most intimidating or mysterious. They will execute a structured explanation request, use the 'zoom' technique to dissect it from high-level flow to line-by-line syntax, and then perform a quick mental test run of the code. The objective is not for them to memorize syntax, but to gain the confidence that they can decrypt and navigate any file their AI companion produces.

tasks: Highlight an unfamiliar snippet of code and request a structured, line-by-line logical explanation from the assistant.

sessions.title: Recognizing Dependencies and Configuration Files
sessions.description: Read package manifests (like package.json) to understand how external tools, plugins, and helper assets are imported.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin this session with a simple but powerful analogy to anchor the concept of external software dependencies. Ask the audience to imagine building a modern restaurant. A chef does not grow their own wheat, mill their own flour, or forge their own copper pans; they rely on trusted external suppliers. In the same way, modern software developers—and especially Vibe Coders—rarely build everything from scratch. They rely on external code libraries called dependencies. This session is designed to demystify how these external tools are cataloged and stabilized, transforming what looks like intimidating configuration gibberish into a clear roadmap of your application's external support network.

Draw a visual schematic on the whiteboard representing the anatomy of a project directory. On one side, sketch the application's unique code (the custom logic and UI elements we prompt the AI to build). On the other side, draw a 'pantry' box representing external libraries. Connect these two areas with a document labeled 'The Manifest File' (such as package.json in JavaScript environments or requirements.txt in Python). Explain that the manifest is a high-level shopping list telling the computer exactly what ingredients our custom code needs to run. Walk through the key fields of a standard package manifest on the board: metadata like project name and version, 'scripts' which act as short-cut commands to start or build the app, and the 'dependencies' block listing the names and broad version ranges of external helper libraries.

Now, introduce the critical technical vulnerability of relying on dynamic libraries: version drift. On the whiteboard, illustrate what happens when our manifest simply requests 'flour version 2.x'. If the supplier updates their flour recipe tomorrow in a way that breaks our recipe, our application crashes without us changing a single line of our own code. This sets up the logical necessity of the 'Dependency Lockfile' (such as package-lock.json or yarn.lock). Draw a parallel between the manifest (the high-level shopping list) and the lockfile (the hyper-detailed purchase receipt that records the exact batch, hash, and precise version of every sub-ingredient down to the smallest detail). Explain that the lockfile guarantees that whether the application is built on our machine, a server, or inside an AI sandbox, it uses the exact same external code bytes.

Address a very common trap for beginners: the temptation to manually edit the lockfile or panic when seeing its massive length. Emphasize to the class that the lockfile is a machine-generated document. On the whiteboard, draw a friendly 'Do Not Edit Manually' sign next to the lockfile representation. Explain that package managers handle this automatically when we add or update libraries. Another common misconception to preempt is trying to copy-paste the entire contents of a lockfile or the giant 'node_modules' folder into an AI prompt. Explain that the AI only needs to see the high-level manifest to understand what tools are available, keeping prompts clean and cost-effective.

Conclude the session with an interactive walkthrough of a sample manifest code block drawn on the board. Point to various lines in a mock dependency list and ask the audience to identify which ones are direct tools we use (like a chart rendering library) versus background configurations. Challenge them to find the companion lockfile and explain how it prevents unexpected 'breaking changes' when deploying the application. This hands-on analysis builds the intuitive confidence needed to inspect configuration files alongside their AI partner without feeling overwhelmed by syntax.

tasks: Examine an existing project configuration file and identify standard dependency locks used by the runtime environment.

projects.stage_title: Building the UI and Dynamic Core Functionality
projects.stage_description: Prompt the AI to generate the page structure, CSS styling, and interactive features. Implement buttons to add and complete habits, keep track of daily tallies, and configure local storage so data persists across browser refreshes.
projects.deliverable_increment: A fully styled user interface ('index.html', 'styles.css', 'app.js') that accepts text input, adds active habits to a list, increments completion streaks, and saves progress locally.

exams.title: Unit 3 Assessment: Assembling and Understanding Code Foundations
exams.goal: Assess user capabilities in generating basic markup layouts, adding CSS styling parameters, registering events, handling input storage, and querying AI explanations of active code structures.
sections: Practical analysis of layout blocks, styling adjustments, functional local storage triggers, and logical dependency interpretations.

Interpret standard external dependency manifests accurately.

units.title: Testing, Debugging, and Using AI Safely
units.description: Learn the most critical rule of vibe coding: AI-generated code should be treated as unverified until thoroughly audited and tested. Overreliance on vibes introduces bugs and major security vulnerabilities (such as those documented by OWASP). Master structured functional testing, reading log outputs, isolating failures, requesting focused debugging fixes, and safely reviewing and protecting secrets.

lectures.title: Checking the Application
lectures.description: Establish a thorough, step-by-step verification pipeline to audit the generated user experience.

sessions.title: Comparing the Application with Its Requirements
sessions.description: Systematically review your original MVP goals against the live app to spot missing features or incorrectly built requirements.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by drawing a simple, eye-opening diagram on the whiteboard: a split-screen representing 'The Mirage of Completeness.' On the left side, sketch a humble blueprint of a house with a clear label: 'Requested: 2 Bedrooms, 1 Working Front Door.' On the right side, draw a flashy, futuristic mansion with neon lights, but with a missing staircase to the second floor, labeled 'AI Delivery.' Explain to the class that in vibe coding, because we rely on natural language and fast iterations, we often fall victim to aesthetic bias. A polished UI can easily trick us into believing our application is fully functional, when in reality, critical requirements have been omitted or quietly broken. This session establishes the mindset of a 'Product Auditor'—shifting from a passive spectator of AI code to an active, systematic evaluator of software requirements.

Next, draw the 'MVP Alignment Matrix' on the board. This is a simple, highly effective three-column framework that students will use to audit their work: 'Target Requirement,' 'Actual Behavior,' and 'Gap Status.' Instructors should explain how to retroactively extract their original 'Minimum Viable Product' (MVP) goals from their prompt history. A common mistake beginners make is evaluating the app based on what they *remember* they wanted, rather than what they actually *specified* in their early planning documents. Show how to write down a primary requirement on the board (e.g., 'User can filter tasks by priority') and map it directly to a tangible, step-by-step user interaction to see if it truly exists in the current build.

Introduce the concept of 'Feature Drift' and 'Scope Creep by Proxy.' Explain to the students that AI models love to please users and will often add unrequested, highly complex UI elements—like animated graphs or dark mode toggles—while silently ignoring fundamental structural requirements like data validation. Teach the instructor to demonstrate how to categorize these unexpected features. If a feature is not in the original spec but is fully working, it is a 'bonus' (but must be watched closely for bugs); if it is present but broken, or if it replaces a core requirement, it is a 'distraction.' Emphasize that a successful vibe coder ruthlessly prioritizes core functionality over decorative AI additions.

Conclude by guiding students through the practice activity of building their own 'Custom Verification Checklist' for their personal project. On the whiteboard, model how to take a loose, conversational requirement (e.g., 'I want a simple way to track my daily water intake') and break it down into testable micro-assertions (e.g., '1. App displays current intake. 2. Clicking plus button adds 250ml. 3. Intake reset occurs automatically at midnight.'). The goal of this exercise is to shift the learner's perspective from 'vibe testing' (just clicking around randomly) to structured verification. Warn the instructors to intervene if students immediately try to fix bugs using the AI during this session; the entire focus must remain purely on identifying and documenting the gaps before a single line of code is modified.

tasks: Construct a custom checklist comparing original project descriptions against the current live software state.

sessions.title: Testing the Main User Flow
sessions.description: Execute a structured run-through of your application’s core features, verifying that standard actions succeed without error.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start this session on the physical or virtual whiteboard by drawing a straight, smooth road labeled 'The Happy Path' leading from a 'User Entry Point' directly to 'Successful Outcome.' Explain to the audience that in software testing, before we try to break our app with extreme edge cases, we must first ensure that the absolute standard, ideal path works flawlessly. Many beginner vibe-coders celebrate too early when their code runs once, without systematically verifying that the basic user journey is frictionless. This whiteboard visual anchors the session by defining a standard user flow as the foundation upon which all subsequent testing is built.

Transition the lecture into a step-by-step breakdown of how to map out a user journey without looking at a single line of code. Instruct teachers to write down a simple list of sequentially numbered actions on the board, representing a common workflow—such as adding an item to a cart, editing it, and viewing the summary. Emphasize to the learners that they must step out of their roles as creators and step into the shoes of a first-time, highly observant user. Explain that the main goal of this audit is to identify 'friction points' and 'silent failures'—moments where a button click does something, but there is no visual feedback, leaving the user wondering if the app is frozen.

Introduce the concept of a 'User Audit Log' on the whiteboard, structured as a simple grid with three columns: 'Action Taken,' 'Expected Result,' and 'Actual Result / Vibe.' Explain that a common pitfall for absolute beginners is ignoring subtle lags or minor visual jumps because 'it technically still works.' Teach them that under high network loads or different user environments, these minor glitches escalate into critical failures. Emphasize that logging these subjective feelings of slowness or visual instability is just as crucial as logging hard code errors because user trust is won or lost in these micro-interactions.

Guide the students through a live mental simulation of the practice task. Describe how to perform a deliberate walkthrough of their application's UI, pausing after every action to evaluate the response time and visual transitions. Explain how to document these observations systematically in their logs. Conclude by teaching the instructors how to guide students in converting this qualitative log back into structured prompts for their AI coding assistant. Show how to bundle these usability issues into a cohesive, non-contradictory feedback prompt so that the LLM can refine the interface elements without breaking the core logic of the application.

tasks: Perform an end-to-end user audit of your interface, logging any step that feels slow or displays unexpected results.

sessions.title: Testing Unusual or Invalid Input
sessions.description: Purposely try to break the application with unexpected inputs, like blank forms, massive text lengths, and invalid numbers, to build resilience.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by confronting a common psychological trap in Vibe Coding: the 'Happy Path' bias. When we build applications using AI, we are often so thrilled to see the initial interface working that we only test it with perfect, expected inputs. The teacher should start by drawing a split screen on the whiteboard. On the left side, sketch a neat user typing '5' into a quantity box (the 'Happy Path'). On the right side, draw a chaotic user typing '-999', pasting a whole novel, or leaving the box entirely blank (the 'Wild Path'). The core message of this session is that true software resilience is defined not by how it handles the happy path, but by how gracefully it survives the wild path.

To build conceptual intuition, the teacher will introduce the 'Input Filter' analogy on the whiteboard. Explain how data flows from the user interface into the application's underlying logic. Without validation rules, raw input goes straight to the engine. If a user inputs letters where a number belongs, the logic engine gets confused and crashes. Draw a sieve or funnel on the board representing 'Input Validation'. Explain that validation acts as a polite security guard, checking everyone's credentials before letting them enter the application. For beginners, understanding that they must explicitly instruct the AI to build this guard is a major eye-opener, as AI models often omit comprehensive validation in their first drafts to keep code simple.

Next, the teacher should map out three classic categories of disruptive inputs on the board, explaining the logic of why they fail. First are 'Empty or Null' inputs, where clicking submit on a blank form can cause the database to search for nothingness and freeze. Second are 'Boundary and Extreme Values'—for example, entering a quantity of zero or a negative number. The teacher can use a dramatic real-world scenario: if an online store allows a quantity of '-2' shirts at $20 each, a weak application might calculate the total as -$40 and theoretically refund the customer during checkout! Third are 'Type Mismatches', such as typing emojis or letters into a numeric age field. Visually linking these input errors to real-world logical consequences makes the importance of testing tangible and urgent.

Now, transition to the guided practice. The teacher will instruct students to actively play the role of a 'friendly hacker' on their own applications. They should run their app, open their input forms, and systematically input zero, extreme negative values, or random letters, documenting exactly how the application reacts. The teacher must prepare students for a common misconception: that a crash or an ugly error screen means they have failed. On the contrary, explain that finding a way to break your app is a major victory. The goal of this exercise is to compile a list of raw, unpolished behaviors (such as the app displaying 'NaN', shutting down, or doing weird math) so they can be systematically addressed.

Finally, the teacher will demonstrate how to close the loop by leveraging the AI to patch these vulnerabilities. On the whiteboard, write a blueprint for an effective 'Defensive Prompt'. Show students how to write: 'When I input [X] into the [Y] field, the application [does Z bad behavior]. Please update the code to validate this input, prevent processing if it is invalid, and display a helpful, friendly red error message to the user.' Emphasize that we must never allow the AI to silently ignore errors; we must always design a user-friendly feedback loop. This wraps up the session by transforming the raw, chaotic feedback of manual testing into clean, resilient code structure through targeted AI prompting.

tasks: Input zero, extreme negative values, or string characters into numeric input forms and log how the application reacts.

sessions.title: Checking Different Screen Sizes
sessions.description: Use responsive dev tools to inspect layout presentation on mobile, tablet, and desktop viewports, requesting design fixes as needed.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this whiteboard session by introducing the concept of screen diversity and layout liquidity. In the era of vibe coding, creators often build applications while viewing them on a standard desktop browser window. However, users experience software on a vast spectrum of hardware—from ultra-wide monitors to narrow smartphone screens. To illustrate this, the teacher should sketch a simple desktop layout on the whiteboard: a wide container with three columns side-by-side. Then, draw a narrow rectangle representing a mobile screen and ask: 'What happens to these three columns when we squeeze them into this narrow space?' This visual setup introduces the core challenge of responsive design without diving into complex CSS jargon, shifting the student's mindset to see their app as a fluid container rather than a rigid poster.

Next, we introduce the browser's developer tools as our primary diagnostic window. The teacher will demonstrate how to access these tools (using a quick keyboard shortcut or right-clicking to 'Inspect') and toggle the device simulation mode. We explain this not as a tool for writing code, but as an interactive sandbox. On the whiteboard, draw a mockup of the responsive simulation toolbar, pointing out how dragging the handles to change the width allows us to observe the interface bending, wrapping, or breaking in real-time. This concept of active viewport testing is crucial: vibe coders don't wait for users to report broken layouts; they proactively stress-test the design boundaries themselves.

We then categorize the common 'responsive layout failures' that students need to watch out for during this audit. On the whiteboard, list the big three visual bugs: 'The Spillover' (where text overflows its box and clips out of view), 'The Squish' (where buttons or input fields shrink so much they become unclickable), and 'The Stack-Up' (where elements awkwardly overlap each other because they lack room). The teacher explains that when these bugs occur, students do not need to figure out how to write CSS media queries. Instead, their job is to precisely document these visual failures. For example, rather than telling the AI 'make it responsive,' the student should describe the exact symptom: 'On screen widths under 400px, the submit button overlaps the input field.'

Finally, we transition to a guided simulation practice. The teacher directs the class to shrink their simulated viewport down to a typical mobile width (e.g., 375 pixels wide) and carefully scroll through their application. Students are taught to look for horizontal scrollbars—the ultimate indicator of a layout failure on mobile—and spot clipped text or cramped tap targets. This hands-on exercise empowers non-technical creators to identify exactly where the visual harmony breaks, write a descriptive feedback prompt for the AI, and watch the AI apply surgical CSS adjustments to make the application look polished and professional on any device.

tasks: Simulate a mobile phone screen width and audit your application layout for overlapping text or clipping boxes.

lectures.title: Fixing Problems
lectures.description: Acquire diagnostic frameworks to locate, explain, and safely patch software failures.

sessions.title: Reproducing a Problem
sessions.description: Document the exact conditions, keys, and navigation pathways required to reliably trigger an active software error.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by introducing a fundamental mindset shift for the 'vibe coding' era: debugging is not a game of guessing, but a disciplined practice of scientific observation. In traditional development, programmers spend hours tracing lines of code; in vibe coding, because we rely on AI to generate the implementation, our primary value is being an exceptionally clear-eyed observer. Explain that when a feature breaks, the natural instinct is to immediately prompt the AI with 'it's broken, fix it' or throw raw chunks of code back at it. Warn the audience that this is a trap that leads to bloated, messy, and circular code generations. To get a precise fix, we must first learn how to capture the 'ghost'—meaning we must reproduce the bug reliably on demand. If we cannot reliably trigger the error, we cannot prove to ourselves or the AI that we have actually resolved it.

Draw a clean timeline on the whiteboard to visualize the concept of 'Application State.' Represent the application as a series of connected boxes starting from a fresh page load (State 0). Each action the user takes—clicking a button, entering text, or resizing a browser window—acts as a transition arrow to a new state. The bug itself is represented as a trapdoor (State Broken) at the end of a highly specific sequence of actions. Use this visualization to explain why the AI needs the exact path: if you only show the AI the broken state, it has to guess which of the dozens of possible corridors you walked down to get there. By mapping the transition sequence, we isolate the exact logic or style rule that cracked under pressure.

Introduce the anatomy of a perfect, deterministic bug recipe. Teach the students the three core elements of a professional reproduction guide: the baseline configuration, the precise navigation path, and the payload or data used. Address the common pitfall where non-technical creators write long, conversational narratives detailing their frustration rather than mechanical actions. Contrast a useless, vague report like 'the form broke when I tried to submit' with a structured, step-by-step reproduction path. Show how structured steps remove ambiguity and give the AI engine the clear constraints it needs to generate a clean, surgical patch without breaking surrounding features.

Walk through a concrete case study on the whiteboard: an interface layout error where a navigation menu overlaps with a logo on smaller screens. Explain how to document this visually and behaviorally. Step 1 is establishing the viewport (e.g., 'Resize the browser window to mobile width, under 480 pixels wide'). Step 2 is the trigger action (e.g., 'Click the hamburger menu icon once to expand the drawer'). Step 3 is documenting the collision (e.g., 'Observe that the close button is hidden beneath the main logo header'). Show how this three-step guide tells the AI exactly where to look in the CSS stylesheet, turning a vague styling headache into a simple, layout-constraint fix.

Conclude the session by launching the practice challenge. Ask the students to write a clear, 3-step reproduction guide for a target interface layout error. Instruct the teacher to evaluate these guides by playing the role of an unthinking computer: follow the student's steps literally, exposing any missing setup parameters or vague terminology (like 'scroll down a bit' or 'enter some text'). This interactive critique will demonstrate how precision in human communication directly dictates the quality of the AI's technical response.

tasks: Write a clear, 3-step reproduction guide that consistently produces a target interface layout error.

sessions.title: Reading Error Messages
sessions.description: Learn to read browser console stack traces and server execution logs to pinpoint lines and files causing crashes.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Welcome to Session 4.2.2. Today, we are demystifying the intimidating wall of red text known as the 'error message.' For beginners, seeing a program crash or open a console filled with red warnings can trigger immediate anxiety. In this public-lecture style whiteboard session, we will break down error messages not as signs of personal failure, but as precise, friendly roadmaps provided by the computer to tell you exactly where it got lost. Think of an error message as a high-tech medical triage report; our goal today is to learn how to scan it, extract the vital diagnostic coordinates, and ignore the surrounding noise.

First, let's draw a whiteboard visualization of what happens when a program runs and fails. I will sketch a stack of blocks representing the 'Call Stack' or execution history. When Code Block A calls Code Block B, which in turn calls Code Block C, they stack upward. If Code Block C encounters an issue it cannot handle—say, trying to read a variable that does not exist—it panics and drops the ball. The program stops, and it dumps this entire stack onto your screen. This is a 'stack trace.' The crucial concept to teach here is that the error is read from top to bottom: the very top block represents the exact line where the program finally collapsed, while the blocks below represent the path of execution that led there. 

Next, we will focus on finding the two golden coordinates inside any error log: the 'What' and the 'Where.' I will write a mock browser developer tools console error on the board: `Uncaught TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'textContent') at updateUI (app.js:42:15)`. We will dissect this line-by-line. The 'What' is the error type (`TypeError`) and its plain-English description (we tried to read something from an object that is empty/null). The 'Where' is the file name (`app.js`), the line number (`42`), and the character position (`15`). By circling these on the board, we show students that they do not need to understand every obscure computer term to identify the exact file and line causing the headache.

A major pitfall for vibe coders is looking at a massive stack trace containing fifty lines of text and assuming they have to read all of them. Most of those lines belong to external libraries or browser internals that you did not write. We will teach students the art of 'tunnel vision filter': scanning down the stack trace specifically looking for their own files (like `index.html` or `main.js`) and ignoring lines referencing `react-dom` or `chunk-vendors`. We will also address the misconception that the line of code that threw the error is always the code that contains the conceptual bug. Sometimes, line 42 crashed because line 10 passed it bad data earlier. Emphasize that finding the crash site is the first step, not necessarily the entire solution.

To wrap up, we will transition into our interactive whiteboard exercise. I will present a chaotic, realistic browser console log containing nested framework references. The student's task is to filter out the noise, identify the specific file path, detect the line number, and deduce the basic syntax or reference error source. This exercise aims to reveal whether the student can maintain composure, locate the user-authored code within a framework stack trace, and translate the error's raw data into a clear diagnostic report that they can eventually feed directly to their AI vibe-coding companion.

tasks: Identify the file path and specific syntax error source from a sample browser developer tools log message.

sessions.title: Isolating the Source of an Error
sessions.description: Narrow down bugs by stripping away unrelated systems, identifying whether issues stem from layout styling, logic rules, or data saving.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by introducing a powerful conceptual model: the 'Divide and Conquer' method of debugging, using a simple physical metaphor. When a light bulb fails to turn on, we do not immediately rewire the house; we check if other lamps are working, whether the bulb works in another socket, or if the breaker has tripped. In web applications, bugs present a similar puzzle. Learners often make the mistake of assuming a bug is one giant, indivisible monster. We will sketch a three-part system architecture on the whiteboard: the Presentation Layer (HTML/CSS layout styling), the Logic Engine (JavaScript logic rules), and the Storage Vault (browser LocalStorage). By visualizing these three components as distinct rooms in a house connected by pipes, we show how an error in one room can be isolated by checking the pipes. This visual establishes the foundational intuition that every bug has a specific, limited address.

Next, the lesson transitions into a diagnostic walkthrough designed to demystify how these three layers interact and fail. We present a scenario where a user clicks a 'Save' button, but their newly customized dashboard widget disappears upon page refresh. A novice vibe coder's instinct is to prompt the AI with: 'The save button is broken, fix it.' This often results in the AI rewriting massive chunks of working code, introducing new bugs. Instead, we teach teachers to guide students through tracing the data flow step-by-step. Is the visual button rendering correctly and registering the click? (Presentation) Is the script successfully capturing the user input and formatting it? (Logic) Is the data actually being committed to the browser's disk? (Storage) We show how to test each boundary using simple, non-technical probing actions, such as checking if temporary changes appear on screen before refreshing, which instantly isolates the Logic from the Storage.

To prevent the common pitfall of 'blind symptom chasing'—where learners change random CSS or JS variables hoping for a miracle—we introduce a structured diagnostic framework. We map out the 'State Check' technique on the whiteboard. Teachers will demonstrate how to use basic browser tools to inspect local storage keys directly. If the storage is empty, the bug lies in the logic script failing to write data. If the storage contains the correct data but the screen is blank, the bug lies in the logic script failing to parse the data or the CSS hiding the elements. This binary branching logic empowers non-technical creators to confidently point to the broken pipeline link before asking the AI for help.

We conclude with an active practice session centered on a hands-on isolation exercise. Students are presented with an interactive mock application where entering a username and refreshing either displays 'Welcome, NaN' or fails to load the name at all. The task is to isolate this bug down to either script-based logic parsing (such as a broken JSON parser) or a basic browser Storage failure mechanism (such as using the wrong storage key). By checking the stored values directly and observing how the script handles empty vs. corrupted data, students experience the exact moment of discovery where a vague 'vibe' of failure turns into a precise, isolated diagnostic statement ready for an AI patch prompt.

tasks: Isolate a sample functional bug down to either script-based logic parsing or basic browser Storage failure mechanisms.

sessions.title: Asking AI for a Targeted Fix
sessions.description: Avoid rewriting entire files for minor bugs. Instruct the AI to supply laser-focused, isolated edits to fix targeted issues.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by confronting the 'lazy prompt spiral'—a common pitfall where a builder, faced with a small bug, simply pastes the entire error message and their whole 500-line file back to the AI with a generic request like 'fix this'. Explain to teachers that while this sometimes works for tiny projects, it quickly leads to the AI hallucinating unrelated parts of the codebase, breaking working features, or hitting context limit slowdowns. The core concept to land here is 'Surgical Intervention': treating code modification like a precise medical procedure where we isolate the exact sick function, provide only the immediate context, and demand a highly localized, copy-pasteable patch.

To build intuition, visualize the project on a whiteboard as a set of LEGO blocks rather than a single continuous block of stone. When one LEGO block's peg is slightly misshapen, we do not melt down the entire castle; we swap out just that block. Instruct teachers to draw a diagram showing a 'Monolithic Prompt' (massive context, high noise, high risk of regression) versus a 'Surgical Prompt' (narrow context, raw error trace, explicit constraint to modify only a specific range of lines). This visual contrast is crucial for concept-first learners to appreciate that 'less is more' when talking to LLMs during debugging.

Next, introduce the Anatomy of a Targeted Debugging Prompt. This structure consists of three non-negotiable elements: the System Context (the single function or file segment causing the issue), the Evidence (the exact error trace or broken visual behavior), and the Boundaries (explicit negative constraints, such as 'Do not alter the HTML layout' or 'Only return the modified javascript function'). Walk through a scenario where a local storage utility fails to parse a JSON string. Show how providing the single offending function alongside the traceback helps the AI focus entirely on adding a robust try/catch block rather than rewrite the entire UI rendering engine.

Address a major learner misconception: the belief that the AI always remembers the exact state of the project from five prompts ago. Explain to teachers how to guide learners to re-verify state within the prompt itself. We introduce the practice of 'Context Anchoring'—always telling the AI, 'You previously wrote this specific block; do not change any variables outside of it.' This prevents what we call 'API drift,' where the AI fixes the bug but silently renames variables or changes utility methods that other parts of the application rely on.

To bring this session to a practical close, guide teachers to run an interactive exercise where learners are handed a simulated, buggy function along with a raw terminal error log. Instead of writing code, the learners' task is to draft the ultimate diagnostic prompt. The prompt must successfully restrict the AI's output to a maximum of 10 lines of updated code. This practice reveals whether learners can distinguish between noisy context and essential diagnostic details, ensuring they master the art of whispering to the AI with clinical precision before they return to building.

tasks: Author a precise prompt containing an error trace that requests a surgical function fix instead of replacing the entire script.

sessions.title: Verifying That the Fix Works
sessions.description: Re-run original reproduction steps to verify that issues are resolved and ensure no new styling or functional bugs were introduced.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by addressing a classic trap in vibe coding: the temptation to immediately celebrate a visual fix and move on without proper verification. This session focuses on establishing a disciplined protocol to prove that the code actually works under pressure. The core idea is that a bug is not officially 'fixed' when the AI says it is, or even when the main screen stops looking broken; it is only resolved when we successfully run it through the exact gauntlet that broke it in the first place, and verify that no secondary systems were broken in the process. This concept-first approach relies on a mental framework of 'Active Verification' rather than passive observation.

To visualize this process, we draw a 'Verification Split-Screen' on the whiteboard. On the left side, we write down the exact reproduction steps we documented in Session 4.2.1, along with the edge-case inputs that originally caused the crash. On the right side, we list the adjacent features that might have been impacted by the new code changes—such as user data saving or responsive layouts. The logic chain is simple: first, we attempt to break the patched app using the old inputs to ensure the specific bug is dead. Second, we perform a quick sanity check on surrounding features to catch regression bugs. Instructing teachers to draw these two columns helps students see that verification is a deliberate, dual-track mission rather than a random clicking exercise.

Next, we address the common mistake of 'selective testing.' Beginners often test only the easiest happy path, ignoring the boundaries. For example, if a bug occurred because a user inputted special characters into a form, testing the fix with the name 'John' does not prove the fix works; we must test it with the original breaking string, like 'J0hn_#1'. The teacher should emphasize that we are actively trying to make the code break again. If the app handles the bad input gracefully without throwing red errors in the developer console, only then do we check off the primary fix.

We then transition to the practice phase, where learners will run validation checks on a patched build. The goal of this exercise is to help students build a habit of structured testing. Instead of just looking at the screen, they are instructed to open their developer console, execute the edge-case inputs that previously crashed the app, and confirm that the execution flows cleanly. By forcing them to look behind the scenes at the console logs during this verification step, we demystify the internal state of their software and build deep intuition for application stability.

tasks: Execute validation checks on a patched build and prove that edge inputs are now processed cleanly without triggering errors.

lectures.title: Safety and Responsible Use
lectures.description: Apply OWASP safety mindsets to identify risk factors, secure private details, filter library dependencies, and verify generated outputs.

sessions.title: Protecting Passwords and Secret Keys
sessions.description: Identify credentials, passwords, and API keys. Learn why committing keys directly to public files leads to server hijacking.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by addressing a silent but catastrophic habit in modern 'vibe coding': hardcoding credentials. When developers write code using natural language prompts, AI models often eagerly spit out completed, ready-to-use code blocks that contain placeholder strings or, worse, real API keys directly embedded in the source code. To make this immediate and tangible, the teacher will sketch a high-level whiteboard diagram of a lockbox on a public street. Hardcoding an API key is the equivalent of writing the combination to your home safe directly on your front door. The core concept to land here is that files in modern web development are meant to be shared, uploaded, and sometimes publicly hosted, while secret keys must remain private, localized, and completely decoupled from your codebase.

Next, we introduce the mechanism of API key theft. The teacher will walk through a scenarios-based explanation of how automated public bots scour code repositories like GitHub, looking specifically for patterns that resemble keys (e.g., long alphanumeric strings starting with 'sk-'). A common developer misconception is believing that a private repository or a minor project is 'too insignificant' to be targeted. The teacher will counter this by showing that automated script sweeps take milliseconds and do not care about the size or fame of the application. If a key is exposed, within minutes, malicious actors can hijack the associated services, spawning massive, unexpected bills on open-source LLM platform accounts or cloud infrastructures. This provides a natural segue to explaining the 'credential' boundary: code is logic, keys are identity.

To build a functional intuition for a zero-to-one developer, the whiteboard will transition to showing how we isolate these secrets using environment variables. The teacher will illustrate this as a partition wall: on the left side is the application code, which asks for a config value dynamically; on the right side is a local, hidden file (typically a `.env` file) that contains the actual sensitive value. The teacher will explain how the code references this secret using standard system variables, meaning the code itself remains safe to share, publish, or hand back to the AI. A major pitfall to highlight here is when beginners accidentally commit their `.env` files to cloud storage or git tracking. The teacher will visually demonstrate the role of a `.gitignore` file, explaining it as a list of 'do not touch' instructions that ensures secret configuration files never leave the local machine.

Finally, we engage in an interactive walkthrough exercise. The teacher will display a sample mock code block containing a hardcoded stripe or OpenAI API key. The class will work together to surgically extract this credential, write a local `.env` definition, and rewrite the original code to fetch the value dynamically using the system environment. This exercise is specifically designed to demystify how software reads configuration without looking at the raw code. It reframes safety not as a dry checklist, but as an essential 'vibe coding' protocol that keeps experimental web creations secure from day one.

tasks: Recognize API key credentials in a sample code block and demonstrate how to move them out of source directories into separate, untracked locations.

sessions.title: Protecting Personal and User Data
sessions.description: Understand basic data privacy safety. Avoid saving unencrypted personal data in places where it can be leaked publicly.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by addressing a massive misconception common among absolute beginners and hobbyists: the belief that 'since my app is just a small prototype, data privacy doesn't matter.' As a teacher, you must frame this session not as a compliance lecture, but as a design-thinking exercise. Use a simple whiteboard drawing of a bucket to represent your app's database. Explain that every piece of sensitive information we collect—be it a real name, email, physical address, or chat history—is like pouring water into this bucket. If the bucket leaks, or if someone knocks it over, we are liable. Therefore, the absolute safest way to handle sensitive data is simply not to collect it in the first place. This concept, known as Data Minimization, is the gold standard of responsible development.

Now, translate this concept into how we communicate with AI. When we ask an AI to design a database or a file structure for storing user data, the AI will often default to standard, bloated templates it has seen in corporate enterprise training data. For example, if you ask an AI to 'make a user signup form,' it might generate fields for phone numbers, birthdays, and security questions out of habit. Show on the whiteboard a comparison between a 'Default AI Schema' (bloated, high-risk) and a 'Minimized Vibe Schema' (lean, low-risk). Teach the students how to actively challenge the AI's suggestions. A great prompt trick to teach here is: 'Simplify this database schema to only store what is strictly necessary for the core utility of the app. Strip out all personally identifiable information (PII).'

Next, walk the students through the design of a schema for a local app—for instance, a personal mood tracker or a simple journal. On the board, write down a list of potential data points: Journal Entry Text, Exact Location Coordinates, User Email, Date and Time, and Profile Picture. Guide them to evaluate each point. Do we really need their email if the app runs entirely on their local browser? No. Do we need their precise GPS coordinates, or is a generic timezone enough? This process of questioning reveals that many application features can function perfectly fine with anonymized or localized keys. It prevents the major pitfall of students creating accidental security liabilities in their early hobby projects.

To wrap up the session, introduce the hands-on practice. Instruct the students to look at a typical, over-engineered data schema provided by an AI. Their goal is to act as the chief auditor. They will sketch a redesigned, minimized schema that accomplishes the exact same product goal but cuts down the data footprint by at least fifty percent. Explain that by mastering this mental filter, they ensure their 'vibe coded' projects remain lightweight, ethical, and safe from the start, without needing to configure complex database encryption protocols.

tasks: Design a data schema for a local app that minimizes the collection of sensitive user records.

sessions.title: Reviewing Packages and Dependencies
sessions.description: Identify vulnerable packages. Instruct AI to verify dependencies and evaluate external code sources before importing them blindly.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this whiteboard-style session by addressing a silent threat in vibe coding: the temptation to trust whatever libraries or external packages the AI suggests. When we use AI to solve a complex coding problem, it will often say, 'Just install this library to handle it.' In a public lecture setting, we want to frame this with a powerful analogy.
